utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Can we have the witness for today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Please remind the witness he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Dordic, may I remind you that you are still on your oath?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: May we have the appearances please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Teresa McHenry. I am here with lead counsel, Mr. Eric Ostberg, co-counsel, Mr. Giuliano Turone, and our case manager, Ms. Elles van Dusschoten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we have the Defence appearances? MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honours. I am Edina Residovic, defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. Defending Mr. Delalic with me is Professor Eugene O'Sullivan, Professor from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honour. I appear on behalf of Zdravko Mucic in this case. My leading counsel is out of town on business in morning. I anticipate his return later in the week. MR. KARABDIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honours. I am Salih Karabdic, representing Mr. Hazim Delic. With me in the team is Mr. Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am John Ackerman, appearing on behalf of Esad Landzo. With me on his team is Cynthia McMurrey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The Prosecution is still continuing with its examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Good morning, Mr. Dordic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (in interpretation): Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, last Thursday during your testimony, which was not completed, you had indicated that some time in July you believed you learned that Mr. Mucic was the Commander of the camp. While you were at the camp, did you receive any information concerning who was above Mr. Mucic regarding the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was said in the camp that the Commander of the army --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. The witness is not speaking from personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Let him answer the question. I don't know what his personal knowledge is. Let him answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Did we have the translation? Was the translation even finished? I'm sorry, sir. Would you please continue with your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I heard, the Commander of the operational group who was above Pavo Mucic was Zejnil Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. Twice now he has said he has heard, and it was said. He is not speaking from personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I don't know what you call personal knowledge. That is what I mean. Except you ask him further how he got to know ... Personal knowledge can be from hearing, from reading, not only from communications to him. Except he should inform the panel which made the appointment ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I will clarify the matter. Sir, can you please tell us how you heard that Mr. Delalic was the higher up person for the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the information that we learned about people who were in charge of the camp was mostly through people who contacted with the guards, like Zaro Mrkajic. Mostly he would tell us who was the superior. There was no way for us to check, because we had no contact with anyone in the camp administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I renew the objection. He is saying that Zaro Mrkajic was telling people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think it is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you ever hear the guards say who the boss was or who was in charge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we were starved for about 90 hours I think Esad Matic, who was a guard there, said that when we got food it was that Mr. Delalic had returned and that it was thanks to him that we got the food, so obviously he was somebody who was above the camp administration. He had been away somewhere and then he returned.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Besides using his name, did he refer to Mr. Delalic or his position in any way other than using his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he said the boss had come. The word "the boss" had been used.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you yourself, sir, ever see Mr. Zejnil Delalic while you were at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on one occasion. When I would just come and I was still bringing the food from the administration building I met him as he was walking out of the building. He didn't say anything to me. He just went out and he was wearing a military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Out of what building, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the administration building, where the administration was housed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. How did you know who Mr. Zejnil Delalic was at the time you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew him in town. I had seen him before as one of the well off people in town, and that is how I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you know what business he had in town? Had you seen him at his business?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: What business had you seen him at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, I saw him in his disco, where I used to go often.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, am I correct that you finished last week testifying about the severe beatings you yourself received during the time you stayed in the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you tell me, sir, was there a detainee named Zjelko Milosevic, who was also kept in the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what, if anything, you observed concerning his treatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zjelko Milosevic was brought a few days after me, three or four days, and from his very arrival he was subjected to special interrogations, mainly by Mr. Delic and Esad Landzo. He was taken out frequently outside building Number 9 --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object. He has not proven he saw any of these beatings. He is testifying from no personal knowledge. None of these people are going to be around to satisfy the right to confront the witnesses against you. If he saw --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: We have not even heard what he is saying. We have not even heard what he is concluding.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: One of his statements --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You are assuming he is saying that. At least I should hear what he is saying before I rule on what you are objecting to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, many times it is too late once he has offered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: It is not too late. It will only be part of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So the witness' testimony is not unnecessarily interrupted, it is the case that I will in these circumstances try to clarify it, and if your Honours believe it is inappropriate, they can then strike it, but I believe it is impossible in this kind of situation to get it all out beforehand. Okay. Sir, would you please -- excuse me while I find his response. Sir, would you please continue with what you observed concerning the treatment of Mr. Zjelko Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I just said, he was taken out frequently outside building Number 9, and he was asked various questions, like was he a sniper. That was the main question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to have to renew my objection. He says he was taken outside of Tunnel 9. This man is testifying to what happened outside Tunnel 9. She has not laid the foundation that he has personal knowledge about what happened outside Tunnel 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Let me hear what he is saying.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I have told you I have to hear what he is saying before I rule. I wouldn't rule before we have the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, would you please continue with what you observed concerning the treatment of Zjelko Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I was saying, Zjelko Milosevic was taken out in front of Tunnel Number 9. That means just in front of the door of Tunnel Number 9, so you can hear very well and see what's happening outside, if we were allowed to look. When there were no guards inside we could. He was asked to confess that he was a sniper, that he had killed Muslims, that he had fired at their positions. He rejected all this and, of course, as soon as he said that he hadn't done something, he would be beaten. In his case I remember a piece of cable was used, electrical cable, which was about 2 cms thick and it had a steel wire inside this cable, and every time he was taken out, he was beaten very severely, and later led back in. Then he told us that a long time ago a Muslim had courted his mother. I think his mother was a widow or something like that. Apparently he had hit that Muslim and this was before the war. He said that that had been the reason that they were accusing him of having been a sniper. Otherwise there was no other reason. This was repeated maybe for seven or eight days.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: May I interrupt and just ask you some questions about that, sir? Who exactly -- who would you see present when Mr. Milosevic was called out during these seven or eight occasions? Who would you yourself be able to see at the time he was called out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You are asking who did he see, not who he would see. Who did he see.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Correct. Sir, who did you see present of the guards or the people in the camp when Mr. Milosevic was called out? In other words, who called him out and who else from the camp could you yourself see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was mostly and almost every time Hazim Delic and Esad Landzo were present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHITE
utterances.text: Now who called him out.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Who called him out? Can you just describe what you would see and hear at the time Mr. Milosevic was called out, where one person was, who the other one was, who spoke? Can you just describe this in more detail, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The doors would open. Hazim Delic would be at the door and he would call out Zjelko Milosevic. He goes out and then the interrogation begins, actually beatings. On one occasion a TV station came. They were black people, probably from one of the Arab countries. They took Milosevic out; Rajko Dordic, Desimir Mrkajic as well. They placed them before the cameras, before the TV cameras and they asked that they confess that they had been snipers, that they had killed Muslims. Landzo and Delic were beating -- would beat them when the cameras were off and then the people from the TV team would join in the beatings as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am going to object. He has not said he could see what was going on outside of Tunnel 9. He testified Mr. Delic called them out and then he goes into the story of what happened with the Arab film crew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually you were not listening properly. He said he could see and hear from where he was inside. He said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. So he said he could see and hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. You have your opportunity to test that testimony later.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, at the times -- going back for a minute, at the times that Mr. Delic would call Mr. Milosevic out, could you yourself see Mr. Landzo present on those occasions and, if so, where would he be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me tell you I could see him, because all that was happening in front of Number 9 -- let me make it clearer. It's, for instance, the distance between me and the interpreters over there. So you can imagine that the door was over there where the glass is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: During the actual beatings that you have referred to, was the door always closed or was it always open, or sometimes it was open and sometimes closed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The door was mostly open, unless they banged shut, and they were sort of half closed, but they were mostly open, except that night when Zjelko Milosevic did not return to building Number 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Before we get to that, the times when you yourself would be able to see what was happening outside the door, what instruments, if any, did you see the people have? In other words, you have testified before that Mr. Delic and Mr. Landzo participated in this and that there was a cable. Can you state exactly who it was who had a cable, and if anyone else had another instrument? Could you just please us exactly what you yourself could see through the door when Mr. Milosevic was being beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At one point I saw when Hazim came. He was carrying this cable. Zenga mostly carried a baseball bat.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Zenga carried the baseball bat and Delic carried the cable. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: On these occasions could you actually hear what was being asked of Mr. Milosevic, the questions that were being asked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told you the distance was roughly as far as the interpreters are. So when there is a loud discussion going on, of course you hear very well, especially as it is a tunnel which has an echo, so you can hear voices well inside.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Whose voices could you recognise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The three of them: Milosevic, Zenga and Delic exclusively.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. You indicated, sir, that on one night Mr. Milosevic did not come back. Could you please tell this court what you yourself observed or heard that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, let me say first that that day, the day before this night, Hazim Delic told him that that night at 1.00 am he would go to the toilet. I beg your pardon for using the word to piss.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. This is non-responsive. He is answering a different question from the one that Ms McHenry asked.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: May I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can respond.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I asked the witness what happened and he is providing information which is directly relevant to explaining what happened. I believe the witness should be allowed to complete his answer, and then if it is irrelevant or unresponsive, then it can be struck. In these situations where we do not have a jury and the witnesses are not trained in exactly the specific order that the defence attorneys would like, I think it's inappropriate for the witness to constantly be interrupted. I believe your Honours can understand when the witness gives an answer and explains it, and if it is irrelevant your Honours can disregard it or even strike it, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Along those lines, the question was something about what happened that night. The answer was what happened the day before. Secondly, I think we are all familiar with non-jury trials in our jurisdiction,. Even in non-jury trials we still have things called Rules of Evidence. Just because there is not a jury here does not mean we throw away the Rules of Evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: If his answer does not lead to what happens the next day, then that might be irrelevant, but if it properly connects what happens, then I don't think it is irrelevant. Let me hear his answer and then I'll know what conclusions as to draw.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, would you please continue with your answer and if it is relevant to explaining what happened that night, please explain what happened the night before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And indeed, as Hazim had said, that night -- I don't know what time it was -- his voice could be heard outside building Number 9 and he called out Zjelko Milosevic. Zjelko went out. The door was closed behind him. We heard talk, but this time it was a bit further away from the entrance, so we couldn't understand as well as the previous days when it was just outside the door, but we heard the discussion, later beatings and finally a bullet. That night Zjelko Milosevic did not return to building Number 9. In the morning -- I think it was very early -- we were taken out in groups of five or six to the toilet or rather the hole, and when I went out right next to the hole on the northern side of the hole was Zjelko Milosevic's corpse covered with some kind of a rag or tee-shirt over his forehead with a large blood stain. I can't exactly say what it was but it must have been a head injury.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: When you say it was a corpse, how was it that you were able to determine that it was a corpse? Was Mr. Milosevic moving? How long did you observe his body for? Can you just please tell us how it was that you concluded that Mr. Milosevic -- that this was a corpse rather than a live body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, he didn't return that night. If he had returned, we would have known that he was alive. But he was lying there. We were going out in groups of five or six and there were 30 or so of us inside. All the people that went out, they saw the same scene. He was lying there immobile, with a large blood stain, which means that he was dead.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you just, sir, using the model, show us where it was that you saw the body of Mr. Milosevic? Show us where the hole was that you used for the --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Excuse me. I just want to interrupt at this point because I believe the whole line of questioning is irrelevant. Mr. Milosevic is not in the indictment. It is not a charge included against any of the defendants back here and so this whole line of questioning is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm looking at counts 3 and 4 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am looking at the list. It has several names but Mr. Milosevic is not on there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Maybe I can assist counsel. Counts 3 and 4 of the indictment are for the killing of Zjelko Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I might just have one moment, I have a list summarised here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Will you please allow him to give his evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, would you please show us where it was that this hole was and where the body of Mr. Milosevic was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The hole was just here, somewhere in the middle of Tunnel Number 9. You pass this small concrete wall and it was just here. The body was right next to the hole.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, your Honours. I do want to offer my apologies. Ms McHenry is correct and I am incorrect at this point. Please accept my apology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, was there also a detainee named Slavko Susic kept in Tunnel Number 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That man was brought later too to Number 9. His very arrival to building Number 9 was a terrible scene in itself. I remember well that Hazim Delic was escorting him when he was thrown in. He was wearing a short-sleeved tee-shirt and it was already torn on his back from the beatings he had received upon his arrest and his bringing to the camp. His back was already black and blue. He came in. Very few of us knew him. He looked out of his mind. At first he couldn't speak. He didn't utter a word until he recognised some people inside. He said that he was brought from his home, from his garden, that he was working in the garden when they came to pick him up. They beat him. They loaded him on a car and then they brought him to building Number 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what you yourself observed, either by seeing or by hearing yourself, concerning the treatment of Mr. Susic once he was brought into Tunnel Number 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not long after that Hazim Delic appeared and there were some other guards there. Esad Matic, I think, he was mostly standing in front of building Number 9. Hazim accused him of owning a radio station at home, that he had guided shells to the town, and he was given the same treatment as Zjelko Milosevic. He was taken out, beaten and brought back.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, can I please ask. Can you please tell us exactly in more detail what it was that you yourself saw or heard concerning his treatment? I want you to say who was involved, what you yourself could see, what you yourself could hear while it was happening. Can you just please give us some more detail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were saying he was taken out and he was asked to confess that he had this radio transmitter. At one point he said he would show them where the radio transmitter was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Who would take him out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hazim Delic and Esad Landzo mostly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Would you yourself see them at the time that Mr. Susic was taken out, see Mr. Delic and Mr. Landzo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As I said before, I could see everything at the door. This was the distance, as I have just explained, to everything was happening just outside the door.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Then can you please tell us after he was taken out specifically at this time what you yourself could see or hear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was taken out and taken somewhere. He apparently told them that he would show them where this thing that they were insisting on was that he wanted -- that they wanted him to confess. They took him there. They didn't find anything. They beat him up again and brought him back. After some time he could hardly come in. He was staggering. The doors closed behind him. I went after him to hold him up, so that he wouldn't fall. Towards the very end of the tunnel near the flat area, where Number 9 ended, he was standing next to the wall. Zaro Mrkajic was next to him. He couldn't breathe. He asked for water and I went to get him some water, but somebody else had already brought a glass of water. But he slid down the wall and started to die. We laid him down on the floor, tried to give him artificial respiration but there was no way that we could help him. He was dead.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: What happened to Mr. Susic's body after he died in the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That corpse stayed there all night in building Number 9 and some time the next day, about 11 o'clock, he was taken out.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Talking about the day that he was taken out and then brought back in and he died soon after being brought in, can you please tell us exactly what you yourself saw or heard with respect to that day? Who called him out and what, if anything, could you see or hear about what happened to him? You may have already repeated in before, but I'm not sure it is clear, so I'm asking you to go logically step by step. Tell us exactly who you saw, what you saw and what you heard happen. I'm now referring to the day that Mr. Susic died?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: As far as who took him out, that is asked and answered. From that point on, I would like for him to continue at that point, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Will you kindly ask him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was taken out. As I said, he was beaten for a very long time. That time the door was closed after him immediately. He was just thrown in and there was no further comment and shortly after that he died.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you tell us, if you can, who was it who took him out, if you heard anything after he was taken out, if you could recognise any voices, and who it was who brought him back in? If you know any of those things, can you please explain it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, who took him out has been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Let him give evidence the way he is asked the questions. You don't have to give evidence for the Prosecution. He can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that again, but I will repeat it. Hazim Delic and Esad Landzo took him out. The beating was in front of the building, as I said. He was thrown back in. I don't know exactly. They were probably there. The doors -- the door closed behind him. He was more or less pushed in.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Then at the time when the door was shut and he was being beaten outside, could you hear anything about what was going on and, if so, could you recognise anyone's voices? Could you just tell us what it was, if anything, that you could hear after he was brought outside and the door was closed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly the beatings could be heard and the questions. "Confess. Why don't you confess?" , and that sort of thing. "You were there. Where were you?" That's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were you able to recognise the voices of any of the persons asking him questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it's sufficient that I saw them take him out.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If you couldn't recognise the voices, then you can just say: "I couldn't recognise the voices". That's no problem. I am just asking you if you could or could not recognise the voices of the persons asking him questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were the voices of the people who had taken him out.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So would that be the voices of Mr. Delic and Mr. Landzo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Esad Landzo and ... yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: On the prior occasions before the day when Mr. Susic actually died, can you tell us if you yourself saw any of the beatings and, if so, what you yourself observed of the beatings. Who was involved? Was there an instrument? Could you please describe that and exactly what you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the beatings more or less were reduced to this procedure. The prisoner was taken in front of building Number 9. Then he was turned to face the concrete. He had to raise his arms and they would beat the prisoner, depending on the object they had, a baseball bat, a boot, a fist. More or less the beatings were all the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you specifically remember any of the beatings that you saw of Mr. Susic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that each of his beatings in front of Number 9 I could see, I could observe.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Could you observe anyone actually beating him and, if so, who did you yourself actually see beating Mr. Susic in the days leading up to his death?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. During the time you were at the camp, sir, other than the first fifteen days when you brought bread to the tunnel, did you ever have any other jobs or duties either inside or outside the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the most part not in building Number 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Throughout your entire time at the camp were you ever -- did you ever do any jobs or duties, not just limited to the time you were at Tunnel 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mostly worked when I was transferred to Building Number 6, but that was digging some canals within the compound itself, the trenches and things like that, but one day they loaded us -- I think it was a van and we may have been seven or eight. They drove us to Konjic, to the Bukala section, to Pavo Mucic's house, and there we were clearing a structure. I don't know if a shell had fallen on it or something, but that's what we did. We cleared up that structure. Pavo Mucic was there personally. He was at home asleep when we arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you have any conversations with any member of Mr. Mucic's family at that time? You can just say "yes" or "no" at this time if you had a conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: With respect, I would invite my learned friend to identify what the relevance of conversations with Mr. Mucic's family might possibly be.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would be happy to. There was of a conversation with Mr. Mucic's father about Mr. Mucic's role with Celebici, and I believe that's directly relevant, since his father, I think, would be in a position to know. I think at that time it could be considered reliable. Sir, did you have a conversation with any member of Mr. Mucic's family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I believe a man and I later found out was Pavo's father, was very tolerant towards us. He even gave us some apples, some fruit to eat while we were there and talked to us the whole time. He said that he didn't feel good about what Zdravko -- I think that was his name -- was doing there and that it was the war. The whole war had no meaning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, was there a time when the International Red Cross came to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was on 12th August 1992. The door opened and women came and some men came and we didn't know what it was. I think there was a woman -- she was a delegate of this committee -- walked to the middle of this structure and she just fainted from the stench. We helped her out and the rest of the delegation continued its work in front of the structure. That means the steps of building Number 9, because it was too foul and there was too much of a stench inside for them to be able to work in there. So they registered all of us and gave us these cards, ID cards, the ICRC cards. Even at that time I was not sure that they were the delegates of the International Red Cross, since a lot of time had passed since we were imprisoned and nobody had shown up until then. So we were very reserved, so we only talked very little, only the basic things regarding food and drinks, just the basic conditions of how we were treated there. Then they finished their job and then they probably went to Building Number 6, and a little while later Delic showed up and this man from Foca, whose name I don't know, and started beating just about everybody. They missed just a few. Mostly a boot in the chest. After that he ordered us all to get up and walk out. We came outside and right in front of building Number 9 we sat down into this canal. In fact, we were ordered to sit down into the canal, to face the wall and put our hands behind our neck at that time Hazim summoned all the guards. I have even heard him call a certain Sok, who was cook there. Then the beatings started, mostly kicks. They must have been 13 or 14, these guards who were kicking people with their hands behind their heads, and some of them had boots, some of them had sneakers, and they kept kicking the whole column. It went on for a very long time. I think at first I counted 17 or 18 blows. After that for a while I think I was not quite conscious, but then I felt a very strong kick, which almost threw me into the canal, and then I was ordered to get up and put my hands behind my neck again, and suddenly an order was given -- in fact, somebody called out from this little hill that was behind these two buildings, 6 and 9, and somebody said to get up quickly and to return to building Number 9. We rose as quickly as we could and then at that time I saw from that hill that was between these two buildings Osman Dedic was calling out. I think he was there observing while the delegation was in building Number 6 to inform the others to stop the beatings so that these people would not see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, at some time after the Red Cross had come, were you moved out of Tunnel Number 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I was the last one who left building Number 9. It was the group of 15 and I was in that last group.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately when this was or about how long after the Red Cross visit it was that you were moved out of Tunnel Number 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was late September, maybe even early October. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Where was it that you were moved to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was moved to building Number 6, the large hangar where the rest of the prisoners were.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, using the model and the pointer can you just show us where Building Number 6 is and the surrounding areas, if you know anything about that; for instance, where the guards were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (indicating) Here. We were brought from Number 9 in front of the administration building, which was E, and we were brought over here to object Number 6. There was a guard post right here where this hole is. The other one was across there and there was a machinegun placed there. Two soldiers were patrolling here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: On the hill where you showed the guard post was, was there any other kind of structure or anything there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was a dug-out there when I came there and when I was covering this guard post there I saw it. I don't know what its function was. It was an underground room. I don't know what it was for but it was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, when you went to Hangar 6, were there other prisoners already in Hangar Number 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were mostly people from Bradina and people from the Konjic municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you know who Vaso Dordic is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was he one of the persons you saw in Hangar Number 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Are you related to Mr. Vaso Dordic in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: How are you related?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that his and my father are first cousins or maybe they are third or fourth generation removed. We are not that close.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you know anything about what kind of schooling or what kind of work Mr. Dordic did before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vaso worked in Sarajevo in Alipasino Polje. That is a section of Sarajevo. He worked for the Alhos Company. Later on I think he moved and worked with the railroads as a fireman.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you yourself know exactly what kind of schooling he had and what he completed and, if so, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both of us and his brother were poor students. Neither completed their elementary school, or at least they did not complete it in the regular way.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. After the visit of the Red Cross, was there any change in the treatment the prisoners received at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were no more murders. There were still beatings, maybe less so and less visible, but there were still beatings.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were you yourself ever mistreated after the Red Cross came other than what you just told us about the beating immediately after the Red Cross came? During the rest of the time at the camp were you ever mistreated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. When I came to Building Number 6, the very first night after it got dark the door opened and I was called out together with another I think five or six prisoners. There was a list there and somebody read it out. We were taken out. Immediately after I was taken out an order came to stand against a wall that was really a tin wall. Then the beatings started. I think there was a plank, a square plank, and then automatic rifles. They were cursing me and at some point they threw me back in. I barely managed to get to the place. In fact, I was helped by other prisoners. I managed to get to the place where I was sitting and this was repeated in the second and third and fourth nights. It was the same list. In other words, somebody must have given them a list of who they were going to beat, and the guards were the same: Zajko Camdzic, Osman Dedic, Kemal Mr.ndzic and Kemal Muderizovic. Those were the people I remember. They were like silhouettes in the dark. The next day they created -- they sort of staged a scene as if the prisoner ahead of me had his throat cut. They ordered him to lie down and around his neck area they must have poured some liquid, because you couldn't see in the dark. So I thought it was blood. Then they beat me. I was lying down. They were putting a knife to my neck. They were telling me that they were going to cut my throat. That knife was a knife that was a bayonet of an M-48 rifle, so it was very blunt and it would have taken a long time for them to cut my throat with it. These beatings went on for four nights. It was the same guards and it was the same list. On the fourth night they told me to tell me -- when they told me to get in, I remember the Camdzic guard because he always looked the same. He had his sleeves rolled up and he had a characteristic hair cut, so I could recognise him in the dark even as a silhouette. When I was passing him to get back into building Number 6 and I passed him, he was near me and he put a barrel -- he hit me with the barrel of his gun between the ribs and I fell from that blow, and I lost consciousness. I had a feeling that the barrel just went through me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were there any other occasions, sir, during the time you were at Celebici that you were mistreated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. One day Hazim Delic walked into the Building Number 6 together with Zajko Camdzic. There were some other guards with them. They were not alone, the two of them. Vukasin Mrkajic was designated to be the head of them, and in charge of keeping the order among the prisoners in Building Number 6. I really didn't know what was going on. Hazim was saying: "Who is making some cards?" I don't know. Some people who were there before in Number 6 must have got a hold of some paper and there were some pencils there. So they must have made some makeshift playing cards. So Hazim asked who made those cards and nobody said and then he told us all to turn around, took a shovel and hit everyone in the buttocks with this -- it's like a shovel that is used in a military unit to load the different bulk things. We were about 170 and so he could not hit everyone, so he gave the shovel to Zajko at one point, and then after he took some rest he asked Vukasin who is walking around while he is not there and who is getting up. Vukasin at first did not want to say who it was. Then he ordered him to stand next to the door. There is a small door inside the bigger door at the entrance and ordered him to take his pants off. He did so. Hazim took the shovel and started beating him on his bare buttocks until blood started coming. Then he kept repeating: "Okay. Say who was it, who was it". Vukasin said he will say because he couldn't stand this any longer. Hazim stopped beating him and ordered him to walk around naked from the waist down as he was and point to people who did this. Vukasin pointed to me, among others. Hazim told me to turn around and he kicked me with his boot in the rib cage and, as I said, my right side hurt a lot because of these beatings before and from the barrel of Camdzic's rifle. Then I fell down from pain and Hazim asked for a shovel. Somebody brought it to him and he beat me with the shovel. As he hit me in the buttocks, the metal part fell off. Then he continued to beat me with the handle of the shovel until it broke apart, because it was some old wood. I think it was very old, probably a remain from the army times. When it broke off, he threw the remaining part and he hit me over the back and cursed my Cetnik mother and ordered me to get up. Then I got up and joined the line-up of other prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Other than this incident that you have just described where you were beaten with the shovel, while you were in Hangar 6 were you ever mistreated using any other kind of instrument or device?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During my stay in all or just while I was in Building Number 6?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: During your stay in all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether I described already in my testimony that Hazim Delic also used a device for horses. I don't know exactly what it's used for, but it produces strong electrical shocks. This was more of a toy for him, but when used on a prisoner it inflicts a small burn on the spot where it touches the body like the burn from a cigarette, but the electricity charge is very high. It is not lethal, it cannot kill, but it produces a strong shock, and people who don't know become very frightened. They feel that they will not be able to survive. It is about 10,000 volts, I think, the charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, was this electrical device ever used against you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on one occasion when Hazim took us out for a walk in front of the scales, the kind of island on the road, I was selected from the group and he put me on a stone block on this island.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you please show us on the model the area you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating) It's here, this island, as I call it, right here, but this block was here, but it's not marked on this model. There were three or four of these blocks.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you just describe these blocks, about how wide and how high were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This sort of island is raised above the level of the ground, about 15 cms, and on this area this block was about 30 by 30, not larger than that, 30 by 30 cms.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Would you please go on with what happened to you after you were put on this 15 -- I'm sorry -- 30 cms stone block?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I sat on that block and I begged him not to do that to me, and actually I am a TV mechanic, so I know the electronics of this device. That is my trade. For the benefit of the other people I wasn't afraid so much, but I made a scene intentionally and begged him for mercy. He burned me on the chest.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was your shirt on or off?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was naked up to the waist. This was the time of our walk and when I fell off this block, he caught me by the leg and the device was kept on it for a long time and the burn was quite big. It was later infected, and the scar is still visible.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Sir, am I correct that you have described the incidents where you yourself were the victim of severe mistreatment, that you have finished describing all the incidents where you yourself were the victim of severe mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly in camp Number 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The entire time you were at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. With the exception of minor beatings and slaps, that is more or less it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, how long did you remain in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was the one but last group to be brought to Musala. I think it was somewhere around November that we were transferred.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. You said when you left you went to Musala. What is Musala and how long did you remain there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Musala is a former sports centre in Konjic. It was also a camp in which people were detained. I stayed in Musala until 4th October 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: During the time that you were at Celebici and then the time that you were Musala, were you ever charged with any offences, formally charged or brought to trial or anything like that that you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. I'm almost finished. Just to go back for a couple of minutes, sir, this electrical device that you testified that Mr. Delic used on you, did you ever observe whether or not this device was used on other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On Vukasin Mrkajic. Actually most of the prisoners in building Number 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. The court's indulgence just for one minute. Thank you, your Honours. Direct examination is concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Ms McHenry, in which count does his name occur specifically?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Thank you. 42 and 43. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Any cross-examinations and the order in which you have agreed to take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours. We will proceed in the following way. First, counsel for Mr. Delic; second, counsel for Mr. Mucic; third, counsel for Mr. Landzo; and, fourth, counsel for Mr. Delalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Moran, you can cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Your Honour, can you give me a second to get situated? Thank you. May it please the court, sir, my name is Tom Moran. I'm an attorney and I represent Hazim Delic. I'm going to ask you some questions. Some of the questions are going to require just a "yes" or "no" answer. Could you just give me a "yes" or "no" to those. Do you think you could do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I'm able to, I will. If an explanation is necessary, I will provide an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, sir, if I ask a question that calls for just a "yes" or a "no" -- let me give you an example. A little while ago Ms McHenry asked you a question. "Were you some place" was the question. According to the transcript it took about two and a half pages for you to say whether or not you were there. I would like to ask you, if it's something like that, if you could just answer "yes" or "no". If an explanation is required, you can give it, or if Ms McHenry thinks I am being unfair to you, she can come back on re-examination and straighten it out. Can you do that for me, just answer the question that's asked? Can you do that, sir? I'm sorry, sir. I didn't hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Also, sir, sometimes I get a little tongue-tied and it is sometimes my questions aren't as clear as they can be. If I do that and you don't understand a question could you stop and ask me to rephrase it so you do understand it, so we can all make sure I'm being fair touch. Can you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: One last thing. You've been nodding your head a couple of times, "yes" or "no". There is a woman up at the front of the courtroom and there is another woman over there who are called court reporters. They have to write down everything you and I say. They can't write down a nod. If you can actually answer out it might go a little quicker. Will you agree to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will and I hope I have answered all questions put to me so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. That's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember skipping any question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I don't think you did. Let me go over a couple of things with you. Okay? Let's talk about Bradina first. As I understand it, there was a pretty major battle in Bradina, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no battle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: There was no battle? Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a great attack but a battle is something else. A battle and a great hullabaloo is something else. One could hear a lot of noise from Bradina like battle but that was the shelling. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: For instance you had a weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: What kind of weapon did you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An automatic rifle of Yugoslav make.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So you had a machine gun?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. It was just -- okay. You had an automatic rifle. Where did you get it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I got it from a relative, from a cousin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Is it common for people to have automatic rifles in Yugoslavia, the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, it's not common.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So did your cousin have a whole lot of those that he was handing out, or was that the only one he had, or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I can't answer this question with "yes" or "no" so please allow me to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sure. Did he have a lot of them he was handing out or did he have just a few or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He gave me one, and how many he had I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Do you know where he got that weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think at the beginning of my testimony I explained this. Everyone got weapons as best they could. They found some way to get them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That weapon you had was a military weapon, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Pardon me, sir? You said "probably"? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, probably, because in the pre-war Yugoslavia only the army and the police had such weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And did a whole lot of folks in Bradina have weapons similar to yours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depends. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: What do you mean "it depends", sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Many people had their own personal weapons, hunting weapons. People had bought them before the war. They had purchased them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: A lot of people had M-48 rifles too, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That's a military weapon, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: By the way, did you ever do your national service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So you had some military training?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In fact, you participated in setting up some trench lines in Bradina, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me tell you, when you look over the hill and you see how many people and what heavy arms concentration is being formed, it is normal that you try to defend yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In fact, there were about 6,500 Muslim soldiers attacking Bradina, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a figure I learned of later in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And there were about 350 of you defending, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And you had a lot of trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. In the area where I was there was about ten -- there were about ten of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And you managed to hold off these 6,500 soldiers for about two days; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that they were not psychologically prepared to enter Bradina for us to hold them off. 350 compared to 6,500 is hardly a number that could resist for such a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, that's what you said in your statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor back on 23rd and 24th January 1996, isn't it? Didn't you say: "We did, however, manage to resist for 48 hours"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how I said it then. I am telling you that in the part of the front where I was there were no operations. The attack was concentrated on that one hill. The centre of the attack was the hill. The rest was mere intimidation of the people who were defending Bradina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let me step back for a second. Let's talk about that statement you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor on 23rd and 24th January 1996. Let's just talk about the way the statement was given; okay? I'm not talking about the contents, just how it was given. Can we do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now isn't it true that there were two people there, a Bart d'Hooge, who was a man, an investigator, who probably spoke in either English or Flemish, and a translator, who spoke to you in Serbian; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: The way it would occur would be that Mr. d'Hooge would say something -- sir, I notice you are looking at your watch. Do you need a break? If you need a break, I think we may be able to arrange it, if you're tired or something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. Anyhow, the way it would work would be Mr. d'Hooge would ask a question and it would be translated to you in Serbian; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And then you would give your answer in Serbian and it would be translated back into whatever language Mr. d'Hooge was using; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And then the answer would be typed in English on a typewriter of some kind or a computer of some kind; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And when it was all over, at the end of the statement, giving the statement, it was all typed up in English and the translator read it to you in Serbian, translated it to you; isn't that the way it worked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And then you signed the English copy; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Did they give you a copy of your statement to keep?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So the next time you saw your statement was when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Belgrade. I can't remember the date exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Who showed it to you in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember the name exactly, but somebody from the Prosecution or appointed by the Prosecution, who asked me whether there was anything I needed to correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Would that be a man named McLeod? Does that sound familiar, McLeod, Alistair McLeod, a man from Scotland?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Besides Mr. d'Hooge and Mr. McLeod, who have you talked to about your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With Mr.s McHenry. I apologise for the pronunciation of her name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, I promise you, you pronounce her name better than I could pronounce most names from the former Yugoslavia, so don't feel bad about that. When did you talk to her about your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During my stay here in the Hague. We didn't really talk about it. We just had the statement and I had the statement in front of me, and we talked about the way things would happen in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: She went over your statement with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. Let's get back to the battle of Bradina. Who was the Commander of the people that were defending the city, the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said it was mostly the people who organised themselves, but, as we say, in every herd there must be a leader, and so it was in this case, too, and it was Rajko Dordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: What kind of uniforms did you wear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whatever we had. Civilian clothes, jeans, shoes, a jacket, whatever we had. No-one had a military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You didn't have any armbands or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now at some point during the battle for Bradina you fled with some other people, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You were all armed when you fled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: By the way, what eventually happened to that automatic weapon that you had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I gave it to some people, mostly civilians in the village of Ljuta near Kalinovic. They were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Those were the people that arrested you; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They didn't arrest us. They just asked us to surrender, to come down, and offered transportation to Kalinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Eventually after you came down and turned yourself in, you found yourself in the custody of the members of the HOS, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me tell you, they promised that they would transport us to Kalinovic. They didn't do that. They said that they didn't because it was already dark and it wasn't safe to go along that road. There could be engagements between Serb and Muslim forces. So they took us back to the village. Then some people with HOS insignia appeared, two men I remember well. One had HVO on his sleeve and the other had HOS on his sleeve.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Eventually you ended up in the custody of people from HOS; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've just told you I don't know whose competence it was. I saw two people wearing these uniforms, one HOS and the other HVO. The others were mostly in camouflage uniforms. They didn't have any visible insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Moran, I think we'll stop and have a break at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: We'll come back at 12 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honour, may I address you before we continue with the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can. Mr. Moran, do you permit us to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no problem with her speaking. I'm afraid to say "no". MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honour, during the break the Prosecution informed us on the possible but not final list of witnesses who night come after the videolink. In view of our own schedule and the need for us to prepare for certain witnesses we would ask, if possible, for the Prosecution to give us first the definitive list of witnesses during the day and also the Prosecution is informing us that it may call up some Austrian policemen as the first witnesses. We would like to know the names and ranks of those policemen, which the Defence will have to prepare for. If we are working all day today, I don't think we will have the opportunity to put this request to you later. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Have you made these requests to the Prosecution? MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, I submitted this request at a meeting last Thursday. We have just this moment received this list. So I'm asking in your presence if the Prosecution could confirm that list during the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I am asking whether the further request which you addressed to the Trial Chamber has also been made to the Prosecution in view of the lists they gave to you?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have not, because this occurred just a moment before your entry, so I took advantage of the opportunity to make this request just before the cross-examination. I apologise if I should have done that before, but I couldn't have done it before because I only just received the list. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: This is an arrangement which you can make not necessarily through the Trial Chamber. I'm sure they'll give you the list you want. Thank you very much. I'm sure the Prosecution will have a reaction to that. You will be willing to give.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Of course, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Of course. We don't know necessarily the list of every single Austrian police officer, but from the testimony we can give them the list of the ones that came out in testimony last week. So we can give them that list also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's have the witness. Mr. Moran, the witness is open to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May it please the court, good afternoon, sir. Let's continue --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good day, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let's continue with where we left off. After you ended up in the custody of the HOS and the HVO you were taken with a whole bunch of people --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I object to that. I don't believe that is the -- an HOS and HVO person were there but he wasn't sure whose custody they were in. So I object to that as a misstatement of the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Frankly if you left him, he could have answered the question as to his own understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, let us try it this way. When you were taken into custody there were some people with HVO insignia on their uniforms and HOS insignia on their uniforms; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They brought us to a school. I didn't say it was detention. They didn't mistreat us or anything. They just took us there. I think I explained that properly at the beginning of my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and you arrived at school some time on 30th May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Were you free to leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I didn't know actually where to go. I found myself in a strange place. I later learned it was the village of Ljuta, near Kalinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So if you weren't free to leave I think we can agree you were probably being detained, were you not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: He said he didn't know whether he was free because he did not know the place. It was a strange place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Were you free to leave? Could you have left if you wanted to, whether it was a strange place or not? Could you have just packed up and left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how those people would have reacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. When you were at the school someone came in and started firing a machinegun; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. An automatic rifle, not a machinegun. There's a difference between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir. So if you would have said a machinegun in your written statement, you meant an automatic rifle; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think I said that. When I said an automatic rifle, it's an automatic rifle. Maybe it was not translated well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I'm sure that can happen. At that point that man ordered you all to lie down and he started beating you; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and that was when those two men appeared with those insignia. They weren't there when we entered the building, the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And they were members of the HOS; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. These two men, and the third person was a civilian, the one who was firing into the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And you got there at 10 o'clock in the morning and you left at 3 o'clock the next morning, and you were beaten all the time you were there; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no, not 10 o'clock in the morning. In the evening. It was already dark. On 30th May when we were brought to the school it was already dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So if it says in the statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor on 23rd and 24th January 1996: "We arrived there at 10.00 am and remained there until 3.00 am and we were beaten all the time", that wouldn't be right, would it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not correct. What is correct is that we were brought there towards night-time. They didn't take us to Kalinovic because it was dark -- I said that -- when we surrendered our weapons. So it couldn't have been the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So that part of your statement is incorrect, your written statement, either mistranslated or something like that; right? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The beating started around 10 in the evening, 9.30, 10.00 in the evening, and this went on until 2.00, 2.30 in the morning, the next day. It all started in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So you were beaten for about five hours at that school; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And was it before or after the beatings that they tied your hands with the wire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the beatings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And then they loaded you on a truck and took you to Mount Igman to the Hotel Famos; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We went on foot for a long time first to the village of Sabici and then to Mount Igman, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. You were put on a truck to go to Mount Igman; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That's where Dragan Vujicic was shot on the truck; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. After the Famos hotel, after Mount Igman, when we were taken in the direction of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. That was a guard who was in the truck with you that did the shooting; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, who was sitting on the side of the truck behind my back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Are you familiar with what an accidental discharge of a weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: When you did your national service, you had training in the use of firearms, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Did that shooting appear to you, based on your training and experience, to be an accidental discharge or a deliberate killing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me tell you. The track was going on a dirt road, which was full of holes. Personally I think that from the bumping the rifle went off. I don't know the reason, because it was happening just behind my back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. When you got to Konjic, you met a man named Jasmin Guska, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we didn't meet him. He was next to the truck. All these people, Sefik Niksic, Diksa, Miro Stenek and many other guards, the policemen, were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: While you were there in Konjic those people beat you, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those guards, but the leaders of the SUP, they did not personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: They just stood around and watched; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You were taken with about 22 or 23 other people from Konjic to Celebici then; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. When you got there, you were put against a wall. By the way, who was guarding you on the way from Konjic to Celebici? Was it any of these four defendants, for instance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. On the road, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: When you got to Celebici, those guards put you up against the wall. The people who had brought you from Konjic put you up against the wall and beat you; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That's that wall that's just inside the gate on the model; isn't that correct, that concrete wall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We were lined up along building number C, if I see well. It was later known as the dispensary. I can show you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, I would appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's this wall here, not here as you have suggested (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So it is the wall on Building Number 22, the building that later became the dispensary; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Did you know my client before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. I don't know who is your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Hazim Delic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but I heard from a friend of mine that Hazim Delic was his supervisor, so I knew of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know my middle name -- excuse me -- my father's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Do you know my father's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your father?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes. You've got no reason to, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Who told you my client's father's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: How come -- remember giving a statement to an investigating magistrate in Belgrade on October 17th, 1994, a man named Simic, S-I-M-I-C?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And you remember identifying my client in that statement as one of the people who was a guard at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You never used my client's father's name anywhere in that statement, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me explain. That statement was given I think about fifteen days after I was discharged from prison, if I understood the date you mentioned well, when the statement was made, and you must understand that at the time I had become free after more than 800 days. So that neither physically nor mentally could I remember all the details or all the experiences that I had in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: But you remembered my client's father's name when you gave your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in January 1996; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And, in fact, Hazim Delic, son of Ibro, is the only person in your entire statement those father's name you give; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told you, one of the detainees, this friend of mine who had worked with Hazim Delic for I don't know how long, he knows him very well. He knew everything about him. So other people in the camp learn very soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Again my question was: in the statement you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor in January 1996 the only person in there whose father's name you give is Mr. Delic; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
