utterances.text: I think so, yes. I can't remember. Maybe there are some others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Shortly after you were brought to the camp at Celebici you were questioned by a group of people -- right -- interrogated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In fact, Sefik Niksic was the one who asked most of the questions, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: By the way, he was a police officer in Konjic before the war, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Was Jasmin Guska there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that moment I do not remember seeing him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let's go on a little bit to your experiences in Tunnel 9; okay? Now, everybody had an assigned place to sit in Tunnel 9, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And were you sitting near the door to the outside or closer to the door on the back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was exactly midway -- not exactly but roughly midway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Was it before the curve or after the curve in the tunnel? The tunnel curves, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. About midway of the straight part before it curves. I'm not counting the part that curves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And the tunnel goes down fairly sharply, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In fact, that's because it leads to a building that can be used as a bomb shelter -- right -- or a room that can be used as a shelter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is my assumption. I know there was a door there and what is behind it I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You said in your statement there was a door leading to a gas station which could be used as an atomic shelter. So you knew there was a bomb shelter down there when you gave your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor back in January 1996; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I said that this tunnel -- that above the tunnel was a petrol station and what is underneath I don't know. I know that there was a metal door and a ventilator on the door, and I don't know what is behind. I said it looked like an atomic shelter. That is what it could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So there was a ventilator on the door in the bottom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The ventilator was built into the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And so when you said in your statement: "At the end there was a metal door leading to a gas station which could be used as an atomic shelter", you didn't know whether that was right or wrong; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know because I never went behind that door. The door couldn't be closed. It was only the ventilator that was used occasionally. It was switched on occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. So there was a hole in the door. It had a ventilator; right? Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, and what was behind that door I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. So let me make sure that I understand this right and make sure that the judges understand this. When you said in your statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor in January 1996: "At the end there was a metal door leading to a gas station which could be used as an atomic shelter", you didn't know that there was a gas station back there, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I went out of Tunnel Number 9 I saw that above this tunnel, behind this, was a covered sort of a shelter that looked like a gas station. So I thought that that was a door leading to the gas station and I assumed that it could be a reservoir or a bomb shelter. Never for a moment did I say explicitly that it was a shelter or a gas station or anything. I was just trying to explain what it looked like. To me it looked like a shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. That gas station you are talking about, point to it on the model, will you? Take the pointer and point to it on the model?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. (Indicating) It is. (No translation).

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't get a translation of that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer, sir. There was some problem with our interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Please repeat the demonstration you just made.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating). This was probably the gas station, or at least that is what it looked like, and if there's a door here, then I assumed it led to this facility, that the two were linked, but what is really underneath I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So what you call a gas station has a letter on top of it. Could you read the letter? I suspect your vision is a little better than mine. Could you read the letter on top of the thing you call the gas station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The letter is N.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is about how far from the entrance to Tunnel 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly the distance but I think it was not much more than 20 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Could you -- could the Registrar show the witness -- I believe it's Prosecution exhibit 2, photograph number 47 and 48. It would be this one and this one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is Prosecution Exhibit 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: We might want to use the ELMO. It hasn't shown up on the ELMO. Is there a problem? While someone is doing that, let's go on to something else. Let's see if we can save a little time here. Do you just want to leave that there and if we can get the ELMO up and running. You testified that the doors to Tunnel 9 was a double door; right? It had two halves of the door?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It was a metal door; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I think we've got somebody here now and we'll see if we can get the ELMO up and running. I want you to look at picture number 47. There's a little number down at the bottom. This is sideways. I think we need to turn it 90 degrees. The picture I want to address the witness' attention to is one that's labelled number 47. Not that one but the other one on the page. That one. I want you to take a look at the picture that's there and also the picture on the next page, which is labelled number 48, and I want you to point to that vent in the door that you just testified about. Take the pointer and point to the door, to the hole in the door that's the vent that you just told us about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating) You cannot see the vent here in this picture but this is the metal door where the ventilator was and this ventilator was turned on and used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Look at the next page, page 48, picture number 48, and see if you can show us the holes in the door that you testified about. If you see there's two doors there, they appear -- see if you can see the hole in the door that you were telling us about. Just point to it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You cannot see it on the door, but I do say that this ventilator was turned on and it was very powerful. It would draw in a lot of air. The ventilator was in the door itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now while we've got the usher here, let's go back one more page to picture number 45 so we can see if we can get this all done at one time. There you go. Would you agree with me that that is a picture of the front of Tunnel Number 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And the doors that go into Tunnel Number 9, there's really a double door. There's two halves; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: One half basically starts where that little white square that says "9" is; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That would be the right side of the door. The left starts to the left of where that plaque is that says "9"; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The left hand side, if you are standing in front of the door, the left hand side starts on the left edge of Number 9. So that would be -- then the other side would be to the right of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: There are several steps that go down to get to that door; right? You have to say "yes" or "no".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It is, what, about 1 metre or 1.5 metres below ground level to get down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't believe that it is a 1.5 metres, but I think it's about 1 metre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. You have never saw that side of the door that has the 9 on it ever open completely, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did. I did see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: When they opened the doors, did they usually open both doors or just one half?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depended. Sometimes both; sometimes just one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And the doors open inward, don't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think they don't. I think that they open outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at picture number 46. That's taken from about where you were sitting, isn't it, about halfway down the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I still think it doesn't -- this photograph here is -- was taken -- you can see it well, the end of this slope. So this picture was taken from the flat section, from the flat area of this room. So this is the very end of it. So you could see the edge of this wall that curves away from the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Then point to where you sat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating) In the middle of the section, so it would be around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So you are about how many metres from the front door?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said about as far as the booths are, so about 10, maybe even less, just between here and the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: 9 or 10 metres; is that a fair guess?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let's say it's that. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Would you agree with me from where you are sitting that the interpreters' booth is about 9 or 10 metres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe 8 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. I think we're done with the book. I think we're done with the book and the ELMO. Thank you very much, sir. When you were in charge of getting the rations for the people that were in the tunnel, do you know what rations the civilians in Konjic were getting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't even know what the soldiers ate in the barracks, let alone what was going on in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Actually you just answered my next question about what the soldiers were eating.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what the soldiers were eating, but I know that a lot of food and other military supplies was arriving to the barracks, that is to the camp, while we were there, and all people who were in Building Number 6 could confirm that, because they were unloading both the food and the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Now you couldn't see that from Tunnel 9, could you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So you really don't know what was being unloaded there, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Until I came to Building Number 6, I was the one who was unloading the food.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let us go through a few things you said in your testimony, your direct examination. One of the things you said was you were hit with a yellowish baseball bat. That was a brass baseball bat; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I understood you well, you said it was brass. I said that at first I thought it was brass because it was shiny, so I thought it was made out of brass.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: But was it wood or was it brass?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The one that I got over my back, I think that that one was wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: By the way, baseball is a big game in the former Yugoslavia, isn't it? A lot of people play baseball, don't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, as far as I know baseball was not very popular there, but that very issue of whether it was metal or not, I understand you, sir you're a professional, but I was not an observer there. I could not have observed every detail which was there. I assumed that it was wood based on how I felt it on my back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: How many times did you get hit with that thing? One, two, ten, 20?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Altogether around 30 times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Were you hit real hard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on one occasion real hard, and I said that in my statement, that I had a lot of fractured ribs from it and I think that the medical record will show that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So when you got hit from this baseball bat 30 times it was being swung as hard as anyone could swing it; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that occasion, yes, when my ribs were fractured.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Just that one swing was hard and the rest of them weren't hard? I mean, I don't understand what you are saying, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were all hard but it's not the same if the bat is swung by somebody who weighs 60 kg and somebody who weighs 100 kg person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Who swung the bat was hitting you as hard as he could -- is that what you are saying -- all 30 times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know the intensity, and I don't know their strength. I don't know how hard they are able to swing. I know how I felt. I know that it hurt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Where were those 30 strikes of the baseball bat; sir? All on your back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Just straight across your spine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depended, and I cannot recall where each blow landed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let's talk a little bit about your testimony on the death of Zjelko Milosevic; okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Now that was one of the nights that -- when they took him out the night he didn't come back, that was one of the nights they closed the door in front of Tunnel 9, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Show the judges again where you saw him being -- you heard him being beat and you saw the body. Take the pointer and just show on the ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Which body are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Zjelko Milosevic, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating) I think it was all taking place on the side here or maybe here, because if it had been right in front it would have been heard better and the corpse was somewhere around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Point again where you saw the corpse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating) Here next to a hole that was dug in as a toilet. He was right next to it in the middle here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So all of that occurred behind Tunnel 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That means along this path or road here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Tunnel 9, which has two solid metal doors that were closed in front of it, and it was around a corner and behind the entrance and above the entrance; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere behind the entrance, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: But you could hear all this clearly, of course?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me tell you, we could not hear it through those double doors that are deep down underground, maybe 2 or 3 metres down. We heard it through the entrance door, which had no window panes, and you could hear everything through those doors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: By the way, you were talking about a -- you just talked a minute ago about a pit that had been dug for use as a latrine. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: When you were doing your national service, did your army teach you, like my army taught me, about a thing called field sanitation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So they didn't teach you that if you were some place with a group of soldiers or whole group of people that you should dig a latrine for people to use as a toilet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. I was in communications in the army and I really didn't have much of an infantry training, and so this thing in particular I'm just not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In fact, when you were doing your national service you were stationed at an army camp where there were a lot of soldiers, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in a large barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And they had a lot of facilities to take care of that large number of soldiers, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Things like barracks and kitchens and showers and toilets and recreational facilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is because there were a whole lot of people that were stationed there; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Now the camp at Celebici was not designed to have a whole lot of people stationed there, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. I don't know what the purpose of this camp was originally. I had never been there before in that barracks. I knew that it existed somewhere behind the railroad station but I didn't know what it was for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Back before the war you didn't see 200 or 300 or 400 JNA soldiers stationed there, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, I had never been in that facility, not in there or around it. I was at a lake which is maybe 1 km away, but I had never been there. I also passed by it on the road and also, to be honest, I was not very interested in it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Slavko Susic, how long was he in the camp before his death?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember exactly. I cannot say precisely the date so that I can tell a very specific time period, but not long. At the most about fifteen days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: What at the least?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe eight at the least.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You testified a while ago about an Arab television crew that came and took some pictures. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And you said you thought they were Arab because they were black people; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Dark complexion and, to be honest this TV crew left a very bad impression on us. We didn't know what it was all about, who sent them, what was it so wrong that we did that the television crews from around the world would come and film us. So psychologically it was very hard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You thought they were Arab because they were black people; right? All black people are Arabs or all Arabs are black people; which is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Objection. Asked and answered. He stated why he thought they were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not difficult for me to answer that question again. As far as I know the world population, my perception and my opinion is that it was some kind of an Arabic group and that that's how these people look.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. I pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any other questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Earlier I announced the order. The order has changed slightly. Mr. Landzo's counsel will go second, Mr. Mucic's third and Mr. Delalic's fourth.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, since Mr. Landzo is going next, it is 12.55. Should we go ahead and take our lunch break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We can spare these five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly invite the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Please warn him about his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Dordic, may I remind you that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Who is cross-examining? After your charity, you have forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: For the five minutes. There is one thing I would like to ask before I begin. The Prosecution and Defence had filed a joint motion for the medical examination of this witness. I was just wondering if we had gotten any results from that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: We certainly haven't gotten any results and I have no information as to whether the appointment has been, in fact, even carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: May it please the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Mr. Dordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: My name is Cynthia McMurrey, and I am defence counsel for Esad Landzo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Glad to meet you.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Nice to meet you. You have been doing such a good job so far about listening to the questions and trying to answer the questions since we have been on cross-examination. I would just like to re-urge you to answer only the questions that you have personal knowledge of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: And those are the questions that you have personally witnessed or personally experienced, although I'm sure the Prosecution has already explained all that to you ahead of time; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: I don't know. How many days have you been waiting back there to testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here in the Hague?

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Here in the Hague.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've been here since last Saturday -- the other Saturday -- ten days I have been here.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: While you have been waiting to testify did the Prosecution or anybody from the Prosecution ever discuss with you why we've had this delay, anything about any videotape or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr.s Teresa told me that a video had been seen and nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Did they discuss anything with you about any newspaper articles that had been published?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly no, but I heard of those articles before I came here.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Did they discuss with you anything about the Association of Detainees in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Just by way of clarification, I'm not sure that -- I'm not objecting to anything, but I am not sure that the newspaper articles you are referring to are the same ones that the witness is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to get into specifics. Thank you. I'm sorry. I didn't get the last answer to the question about the Association of Detainees in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not discuss them here.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Some time in the last few months the Prosecution notified you and told you that the Defence would like to have a chance to discuss your experiences at Celebici with you, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: And you decided you did not want to talk with anybody from the Defence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: I want to get a few things cleared up also. When we talk about statements that you've made, you've given four statements in all, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think three. This is the fourth.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, this -- let us just go through it so I understand what you are thinking are your statements and everybody is clear. The first statement that we are referring to is one that was given before a military investigating committee, the Fourth Corps in Konjic on January 20th, 1993. Was that your first statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. If you're counting that statement as well, then it's all right. Then it's four.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. Then the next statement you gave was the one before Judge Elia Semic in the lower court in Belgrade on October 17th, 1994; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: The next statement you gave would have been January 23rd and 24th of 1996, which was to the Office of the Prosecution; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: And then the next statement would have been November 14th, 1996, and that's another statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecution; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now it's safe to say that during the period since your release from Celebici you have spoken to the Association of Detainees in Belgrade, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'm going to let my learned colleague, Mr. Greaves, ask you more questions about that later. Mr. Dordic, in your statements you have -- first of all, what is your occupation today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just now I am working as a waiter. That's one job, and in another job I'm doing maintenance work on some electrical equipment. So I have two jobs at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: I believe that you said earlier that you did repair work on televisions also, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: And in 1993 you told the investigating committee that you were an expert in electronics; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Then in 1994 the statement from Belgrade says that you were a telecommunications engineer; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a big mistake. I am an electronics technician for Electro-communication. That is the school that I graduated from.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: So then if the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A craftsman, not an engineer, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: So the statement from Belgrade then stating that your occupation was a telecommunications engineer, that's incorrect, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: The first person that conducted the interview from the OTP with you was a Mr. Bart d'Hooge, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Did you get a chance to visit with him back in the witness lounge while you were waiting to testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We didn't talk. He just came by. He was rather nervous. He too was waiting to testify, I suppose. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: So you all just exchanged pleasantries and no discussion about the case or anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nothing, just personal things, just greetings.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now you stated also that you are from the village of Zukici near Bradina; aren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: I want to apologise ahead of time. I know my pronunciations of the cities and the names are going to be absolutely horrible, so if you can't understand, please ask me and I'll try to spell it for you; okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. You went to Bradina, I believe, on April 24th, 1992, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: How far is Zukici from Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 3 kms.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: So it's very close then, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: And you were familiar with the Bradina area before April 1992, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It's more or less the place where I was born, so I know everybody.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: So it would be safe to say that you knew -- you had friends in Bradina, you had relatives in Bradina, and you also worked out of Bradina each day, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: About when did the people from Bradina begin to organise themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know only after this explosion in the tunnel, the small tunnel just below Zukici.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Before the explosion in the tunnel the people from Bradina had set up certain checkpoints on highway M17, hadn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: So it's your testimony today that the people from Bradina did not set up checkpoints on the main road between Sarajevo and Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If they did, they did so just before the explosion in the tunnel or maybe even after. They did but not in the period that you were referring to. In the period around the time that the tunnel exploded. Maybe somewhere around April 21st, when railway traffic came to a standstill and there were no vehicles passing any more.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Under the laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina any time an individual would set up a checkpoint and stop or stall traffic passing between Sarajevo and Konjic, that's against the law, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You want him to give a legal opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: If he knows, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me say that according to the law of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as far as I know, or at least for as long as I lived in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the laws of the socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia were in force and not the law of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. The law of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia would not allow any private organisation to stop or stall the flow of traffic between major cities, would it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, but a checkpoint that was put up before the checkpoint in Bradina was elsewhere, which was also manned by Muslims. Orarbir, this is a place below Zukici. That checkpoint was put up before the barricades in Bradina by people belonging to the Muslim ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: When you say that was put up by people belonging to the Muslim ethnic group, what you really mean is this was placed there by the Territorial Defence. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how they called themselves then. I just know that some companies in Konjic were still working and that it all started with the mistreatment of Serbs in a workers' bus that was taking the people to work. After that the barricade in Bradina was put up.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Just listen to this question too. The Territorial Defence is not just a Muslim organisation. It was a combination of MUP, HVO and the Territorial Defence, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that organisation, nor how it was organised.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: But you did say that you served your military duty, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: And that military duty was in the JNA. In what year was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In 1987.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Let's go back to the organisation of some kind of defence in Bradina. How was it organised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The very fact -- I have already told you this, but I will repeat -- the very fact that the tunnel was mined and that a man was killed in Konjic in front of the Serbian orthodox church in Konjic, people panicked and they were afraid of the further course of developments, and I think it is only normal, and as a result people put up guards around the hills to protect themselves and their families.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. My question wasn't why was it organised; it was how was it organised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that guards were posted on the surrounding hills.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Who were the people who began to organise the defence of Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The people themselves one day gathered in the centre and the question was asked whether we should do something or not, and I know that Rajko Dordic was elected commander.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Rajko Dordic, he's the one who decided how the meetings were to be held and where they were going to be held; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: How often were these meetings held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't attend any one of them, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Do you remember where these meetings were held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly in the social building, social club building or in a cafe. It depends on how many people there were.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Was there anyone other than Rajko Dordic that led these meetings, or was it just Rajko Dordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the late Vaso Vujicic, Dragan Vujicic, they were also a part of that organisation. Then the President of the Serbian Democratic Party, Vukasin Mrkajic, he was there, too, in all of this.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: About how many people would you say attended most of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't necessarily object but I just want to clarify if the witness is answering from his own personal knowledge or what he's heard, since I believe that he has already stated that he himself did not go to these meetings. I just ask for clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll be happy to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Let's hear him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Dordic, you did attend some of these meetings in town, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Town?

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: In the town of Bradina. You did attend some of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a village, not a town. No.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You never attended any of the meetings that were set up to organise the Defence of Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Do you know how the decisions were made at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Would you have accepted that if he answered? Would that be within his personal knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I just asked him if he knew personally and he said no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I just wanted to know whether you would have accepted it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I think this is turning the tables on me now, your Honour. I accept it. Mr. Dordic, when decisions were made at these meetings, do you know how the information was circulated around the village of Bradina? Was there a community bulletin board or was it word of mouth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was mostly word of mouth from one hamlet to another, depending on where people lived. They were informed that on such and such a day they should gather at such and such a place. Mostly it was all word of mouth.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. You stated in your direct examination that you received a weapon, and I don't remember what kind it was exactly right now, but you have received it from a cousin of yours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. What do you mean when you say the direct hearing?

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Maybe I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The examination-in-chief. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: When you were giving your evidence to the Prosecution you stated that you did receive a weapon in Bradina and you said you received it from your cousin; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: What is your cousin's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dragan Vujicic.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Is that the same Dragan Vujicic that was killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: And do you know where he got his weapon or got the weapons that he was distributing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the third time I'm explaining this, but I shall do my best. I said that people found ways. There was lawlessness in all the three groups. Everyone had friends in barracks, in the military factory, and these weapons were brought in by all three sides, the Serbs, Muslims, Croats. It was possible for a Muslim to buy an automatic rifle from a Serb for a handful of money -- this was just before the war broke out -- and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, my question is knowing that -- you did state earlier that this was a military, JNA type weapon. These weapons were provided to the town of Bradina by Serbian officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Weren't they, formally of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Most probably, because an ordinary civilian couldn't enter the barracks. He must have had a friend there or some other way to get hold of a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Now you also said that you did participate in the watches of Bradina; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: What date did these watches begin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told you. Somewhere when the barricades was put up, when the traffic stopped and the explosion occurred, somewhere around 21st April, but I wasn't there yet.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: When you came to Bradina then on 24th April, these watches were already in force at that time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: How were these watches organised? How did you get your assignment of duty, so to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was mostly an agreement amongst the people. In every hamlet or in the centre of the village one of the people that contacted with the people at the meetings who knew what had been agreed and we were all aware of the danger that threatened, and there was no need for any special kind of orders or assignment.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: How did you know who was going to stand watch one night and who was going to stand watch another night? Did Rajko Dordic make assignments for some sort of alternating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we agreed amongst ourselves. As far as I know there was no plan.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: How many people stood watch at one time? Were there four of you? Were there five of you? Were there ten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a very large area. The circle around Bradina is vast, so that usually there were two of us on a particular hill and there would be 4-5 kms between us and the next two.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'm not really familiar with that geography of how many hills are there. Would that multiply out to 15, 30? Just a round figure, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About one-third of the people that we had in all would be on watch duty, and if you were to cover all those hills round Bradina the circle would be more than 20 kms. So one-third, maybe up to 100, not even that many.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Now when you were all on these watches at the different hills like that did you communicate with each other by walkie-talkie or did you have some kind of way of communicating with each other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There was no way of communicating. It was just important to make sure that there were no other people or groups there, but there was no means of communicating amongst ourselves. We didn't even have electricity, so that we couldn't use any electrical devices.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Was Miro Golubovic one of the people who stood watch with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember him from Bradina I just remember him from the Celebici camp. I didn't see him in Bradina.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: What about Stefan Gligorevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stefan Gligorevic was born in Bradina and probably he did keep watch duty, but in the area closer to the other tunnel behind Bradina, so I don't know personally. I cannot say for sure, but probably.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: What about Mladen Kuljanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same applies to him. He is in a different hamlet. His house is just below Ivan Sedlo. This is a mountain crossing. So I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, you have already given a lot of testimony about the fighting and battle of Bradina, so I'm going to leave that to my learned colleague for Mr. Delalic to question you more about. You fled from Bradina on May 26th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: And so from May 26th to May 31st you were basically out in the woods hiding or trying to get to the Serbian area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, you said that you were captured on May 30th near Ljuta; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a village called Ljuta. This is near Kalinovic.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: The leader of your group while you were fleeing Bradina was a Rajko Dordic; is that what you told us? I know you said he was leader in the city but while you were out going to the Serbian safe area, he was also your leader, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what his title was. I know he worked as a teacher. I don't know his training was but I know that he was skilled in orienting himself in the mountains, so ...

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Who were the other soldiers that were with you in that period of time of May 26th through May 30th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please, ma'am, these were not soldiers. These were civilians, mostly my neighbours, my relatives, people from Bradina and Zukici.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Who were the other persons that were with you during that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time when we were trying to escape?

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes. During the time between May 26th and May 31st?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you interested in the names?

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will name the ones I can remember: Mladen Dordic, Zdravko Dordic, Mirko Dordic, Rajko Dordic. I can't recall now all the names.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: People with the surname Dordic, is it safe to say they are related to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but not closely related, not all of them were my close relatives.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Each one of up travelling through the woods from May 26th on, you each had a weapon in your arms, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think that all of them did.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Where were you all headed at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since there was shooting in Sarajevo as well as in Mostar, we went through -- towards Kalinovic, since there was a large military barracks there. So we thought that there the military was still controlling the barracks, and so we wanted to get there.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, on the first night of your travels, on May 26th, where did you all sleep?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly we didn't. We were on the move and it was difficult and those are the high mountains, very rugged terrain. The weather was bad. It was raining. So we found no conditions for sleeping.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, some time between May 26th and May 30th you must have slept some time. Did you all set up camp somewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We didn't have any equipment to set up camp. We only had the rifles and what we -- the clothes we had on. We would take breaks, mostly during day-time, and at night we would continue to move on because they were shooting at us from the hills. They were shooting at our column.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, it's not clear whether you were captured on 30th or 31st May. Can you clear that up for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again I repeat this was not capture. We turned over the weapons to them. They were just shooting at us from the ambushes or however they were shooting. We just came down and gave them the weapons, as if I would now come and turn my weapon over to you. I think that surrender means something else. What they told us was that we would just give them our weapons and they would give us a lift to Kalinovic, but it turned out otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, also some time in that period of time between May 26th and May 30th while you were all in transit you captured some soldiers from the Territorial Defence, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a young man came. I think we were resting in a wood. He came with a rifle and he walked in on us. This was near the village of Ljuta. We told him to show us the way to Kalinovic. He agreed, but he wanted to have us give him an automatic rifle. He was a young guy about 18. I said: "No problem". Then the whole day we walked along some creeks, some other places. I don't know where.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: So this soldier that you say you captured, you gave him an automatic weapon in exchange for his leading you through the forest. Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no. First of all, we did not capture him. We were sitting. It was some cut wood, so there were three stumps. He came and he carried this M-48 rifle. We asked him to lower his weapon and to show us the way. Somebody took away this rifle from him and we asked him to take us there, and as a reward for his taking us to Kalinovic he wanted us to give him one of the automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: But he never was rewarded, was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because we never made to Kalinovic, nor did he stay with us the whole time, because there was shooting in some woods. Two men appeared and he fled. We stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: It was said that two of your soldiers killed this young man, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That young man survived. I saw this young man the following morning when we were led towards the truck tied up. That young man is alive certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: During the exchange of fire while you were fleeing there was a soldier from the territorial defence that was killed, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. The man -- as I already said, the man who entered and was shooting in the air, he said that his brother-in-law was killed, but I don't know who he meant.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. When you surrendered or were captured, whichever way you want to look at it, your weapons were taken from you at that time, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They were not take away from us. We gave it, turned it over. There was no force involved. We just gave these weapons over to them.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: At that time were all your personal valuables taken from you also?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at that moment. I had a small knife. That's the only thing that was taken away. What I had in terms of documents, my own IDs, all this I kept, but at that moment I repeat, only at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: The other people that were with you, their weapons and anything that could be used as a weapon was taken away from them at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again I repeat we turned it in, not just myself but all the people who came down to the road with me. So there was no force on either side. We were met by the people there. Zaro Mrkajic was with them. Nothing happened. We were not tied. We were not mistreated in any way. We all climbed on the truck and went to the village.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Then you were taken to the school in Ljuta; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Men with HOS and HVO insignias came to interview you?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am going to object as to asked and answered several times, both on direct and prior cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just wanted to go through this trip to Celebici because it's very important in this case to explain exactly how many times this man was beaten from the time he surrendered until the time he got to Celebici. I don't know that Mr. Moran walked him all the way through all of the areas that I would like to cover. May I have permission to explore this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You are not going through the process again?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I will do it very quickly, I promise. My question also is -- I don't know that anyone has explained to the court. Can you tell us what HOS stands for? We know what HVO is but what is HOS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hrvacke Oruzane Snage, which means Croatian Armed Forces.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Is that a special group of the Croatian armed forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I don't know, but HOS means Croatian Armed Forces.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Does HVO also mean Croatian Armed Forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. HVO means Hrvacko Vijece Obrane, which means Croatian Defence Council. That is the Croatian army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and HOS is the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia, or that's how it should be, because only these two men had these insignias that meant these two things.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you for clearing that up for me, but when you were at Ljuta, I believe you said you were beaten with rifle butts, kicked with chairs and fists and this lasted approximately four and a half hours; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Then you were taken by truck from Ljuta to the village of Sabici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we walked on foot for a long distance out of Ljuta. I thought we were going to be executed. Every one of us had a guard at the side of him. With them, one among them was this young man that was supposedly captured by us. He was fine. He was with them. We came to a road in the woods and there were two small trucks parked there. We climbed and then we went towards the village of Sabici.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Then you were taken to a prefabricated building and you were beaten there, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was probably the school in Sabici. We were beaten there. These were people we didn't know. After a while they loaded us on to a larger truck.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: I haven't gone on yet. How long did that boating last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. Trust me. I was already a bit lost. I don't know that it took that long. Maybe one hour.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: How many people would you say beat you at that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were about 50 at least who were in the room and the rest were outside. I don't know how many.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: What items or tools did they use to beat you with there? The same thing? Chairs, rifle butts, kicks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Rifle butts and broom handles and things that you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: So anything they could get their hands on; is that pretty accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. . Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Then you were taken from that location to Mount Igman, to the Famos Hotel; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: That's where your personal information was taken, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Personal information and all the ID documents that we had in our possession.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: So at that point they took all of your ID documents and your valuables from you, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: And that was at Mount Igman; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Also to get back into the truck from Mount Igman you were forced to run a gauntlet, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were military only on one side and civilians, including some women, on the other. There were many different objects that they used, but one of them fell and had to be helped up to the truck, couldn't climb it by himself -- could not climb in by himself.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: I want to clarify. By running a gauntlet, that means you were beaten all of the way from the hotel into the truck; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Then you were taken by truck from the hotel to the village of Verdolija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We appeared up there. I saw that -- I have never gone to Verdolija, but I was in Zepe before, but I recognised some people who lived up there who went to school together with me from that village, and we fared the same way in that village, because not that many people climbed on to the truck to beat us. They cursed us and insulted us mostly.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Would it be safe to say when you were driven through this village that there was a mad mob who wanted to stone you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was some rock throwing towards the truck and some beating.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: If the soldiers had released you to that mob, you probably would have been killed, wouldn't you, so it was safer to stay in the truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we were not even offered to get off the truck there. The truck stopped there briefly only.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Then from the village of Verdolija you were taken to the village of Zepe; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Zepe.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Then there was another mad mob in that village, too, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: And then from Zepe you were on your way to Konjic and you were beaten in the truck on the way to Konjic, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. All the guards were provoking us constantly. I think I mentioned this several times. They forced us to kiss some dead boar that they threw on to the truck with us. They said that this was our symbol. They made us kiss the SDA and the HDZ badges as well.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Then when you got to Konjic you were taken to the SUP headquarters, I suppose, and you were beaten by the guards there, too, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in front of the building in the truck.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: And you were beaten with rifle butts, kicks, fists and anything else they could lay their hands on again there; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: In fact, I believe you referred to being treated like cattle at some point, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Not just on one occasion, but throughout my stay in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now could you tell us who the other people in the truck with you during your transport to Celebici were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I already said, there was Rajko Dordic, Miromir Mrkajic, Mladen Dordic. I think I already mentioned several names. Should I try to remember all the names?

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: I was just wondering. There were more people in the truck than were just the people who were fleeing with you from Bradina; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It cannot be more.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: So it was just your group then that was in this truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now when you got to Celebici you told us already that you were lined up against what became the medical building, and then you were interrogated there, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we were not interrogated in front of the wall. We were just beaten there. We were taken individually into the office and interrogated there.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. When you were interrogated, they ask you relevant questions like: "Did you have a weapon? Were you a member of the SDS?" , those kinds of questions, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Based on the answers you gave in that interrogation, they placed you into one group or the other that they considered dangerous or not dangerous. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that that happened later in the camp. There was a process of determining. We found this out later. So there was a contact with the families. They determined that there were -- they ranked the inmates into lighter and more difficult categories.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: But your whole group after your interrogation was placed in Tunnel Number 9, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: And that night after you were interrogated I believe you stated before that someone named Foca, F-O-C-A, beat you that evening, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. I did not understand the question well. When was this?

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: After you were interrogated, when you first arrived at Celebici, were you then beaten by a man named Foca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, at that time I did not know who this Focak was. I was beaten by some people but at that time Focak did not exist; at least at that time I did not know him.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Is it safe to say you were pretty much in Tunnel 9 from May 31st until the end of September or October, whenever you were moved to Hangar Number 6; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, except for occasional times when I was taken to the manhole, but I think that I had already told that.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: So the majority of your time you were at Celebici was spent in Tunnel 9; wouldn't that be safe to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Until the moment when this Tunnel Number 9 was closed down.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. I would like to ask us to refer again to Prosecution Exhibit number 1, photograph number 45, please. If I could have that put on the ELMO, please, Mr. Usher. I know that you saw this photograph earlier, and I just want to -- and you did state that the right side of the door remained closed and the operational part of the door was the left side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the most part the left side was open but the right side could be open as well, and it was open occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Whenever it was open -- when you say occasionally, it was opened when they needed to move something large in or out of Tunnel 9; is that correct -- like the toilet bucket?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That bucket was small enough to be put through just one side. It would depend on the will and the need of the guards. There was no need except to carry in or out of the wounded people. There was no other need.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: So it would be safe to say that 99.9 per cent of the time that door was stationary, closed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry but that's not the percentage that I stated. As I said, that door was opened as needed by the guards.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now could you also look now at Prosecution photograph number 46, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course I can. I even dream of these photographs, actually the things that are in these photographs quite frequently.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: In fact, looking from somewhere halfway down the hall where you were seated out that door, that's the way it looked most of the time from the inside during the day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, unless the other side is not open. If only the left door would be open, that's how it would look.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: It is also safe to say that there were no lights on in Tunnel 9 during the day or the night, were there, as in the photographs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There wasn't except those two small openings at the top of the doors.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: There was also in Tunnel Number 9 -- you had referred to a ventilator in the door back there before. There were fans back close to those solid doors leading to that -- whatever that room was behind those doors. There were fans before that in the tunnel, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand. I did not understand this question.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: If you could look at photograph number 48, please, number 48, this is -- is this taken from inside of the room out towards the tunnel? Would that be the perspective of this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not aware of the double doors in Number 9. I saw one door and then the second door, so I don't -- I'm not clear about the vantage point from which this photograph was taken.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, there were times when you were in Tunnel 9 when you were sprayed off with water, placed back in the tunnel and then fans were turned on. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that happened when we were taken out nude to be bathed, and I can show it to you where. Here is the end of the railroad and there was a cement block that was used as a barrier and there a hose was installed under high pressure and we would come and went running past this hose while --

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Had the fans --

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Mr. Dordic, I was not asking you about your bath. I was just referring to the fans that were in the tunnel. They were turned on occasionally, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, occasionally, and that is one such instance that I was going to describe, if you allow me to.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Those fans are very, very loud, almost deafening, aren't they, when they come on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and very, very strong. They suck up a great deal of air through the small vents on the entrance door.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. I would like to ask the usher to -- I would like to have this marked as a Defence Exhibit merely for identification purposes. The Prosecution has seen it and it was provided to us from the Prosecution. Mr. Usher, could you show it to the witness, please, and could we put it on the ELMO also?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If it has any other witness' name on it, I would certainly ask that it not be placed on the ELMO or that the witness' name be taken away.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Could we put a piece of tape over that witness' name then. That would be fine with me. Mr. Dordic, is this an accurate drawing about the seating position in tunnel 9 at the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly the names or exactly where people sat, but if I can look a bit ...

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes. Take a moment and view it, if you can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think it is absolutely correct, but more or less.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that the closest person to the door is a Desimir Mrkajic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, mostly, more or less. I think later it was Rajko Mrkajic, his son.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: And the drawing doesn't put you exactly right in the middle, does it? It puts you at number 14 down the list, I believe; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If we can just object and at least clarify, this is a diagram from another witness, who specifically stated in it that he's putting down the names that he remembers them but there were many other names, and he gives 25 of them, and he doesn't remember exactly where those people were sitting. So just to the extent that it's clear that this is an incomplete diagram by everyone, and so I think it's an unfair question to ask this witness that he's not in the middle, because the diagram doesn't purport to have even all the detainees on it, just a selected number.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I will accept that from Ms McHenry. It clearly is not totally accurate, but if he can recognise it and state it's close to accurate, that's kind of what I'm looking for right now. So let the record reflect that it leaves off about eight detainees who should be in the line somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I believe it's closer to 25, at least from the witness who drew the diagram. He gives 25 other detainees and he says he can't remember exactly where they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Maybe you just need to clear it up for me. I thought there were 25 in total in the tunnel and he lists 17; is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: During the break I got a copy of this witness' statement and he gives 16 and then I believe he lists the name of 25 additional people. So he gives the number for 16. I have a copy of it here. Then he gives an additional 25 names, which would be, I think, 41 altogether.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, we will be able to clear this up with additional witnesses as they come forward, but just for getting a general picture of where this man sat in the tunnel, I would like to go forward with either letting him recognising it as close to accurate or not close to accurate, if that is fair or not fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You can put the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Mr. Dordic, it shows in this diagram you were sitting about 14 in this row. Would that be close to accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't say exactly that I was number 14. I didn't count, nor did this seem important at the time, but I sat roughly in the middle of the slanting part of the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You were in this tunnel for five months and you never counted exactly where you were down the line?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Objection. Asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I would like to ask the usher to have another document marked just for identification purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Before showing it to the witness the Prosecution would just ask the source of the document and the purpose for which it is being shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: The purpose for which it is being shown to the witness is so he can say this is an accurate depiction of the seating. I'm only going to use the corner picture up in the right upper corner to show him, to see if that's accurately how they sat in the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: May I ask the source of this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: May have I have a moment, your Honour? (Pause). Your Honour, I don't believe I'm required to reveal the source of the document. If he can recognise it as accurate or not accurate, then it can be used for identification purposes one way or the other. We are not introducing it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You can put it to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Usher, I would just like this one corner shown on the ELMO for identification purposes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You must have guessed the purpose for which he is trying to indicate his position. You must have guessed it already.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No, your Honour. If you would receive the document in its entirety, I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You know what is the response for which she is asking him to locate his position.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I think when you see, in fact, the diagram, I don't think that's exactly -- at least, as I understood it, but I am happy to go forward and see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think it is very easy for him to say: "I wasn't sitting in that position", full stop, or "I was sitting there".

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to the prior document, I agree and that's why we didn't object to the prior document. It's this coming up document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I don't see the difference between the two. It depends on how he regards -- if he can recognise where he was sitting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: May I proceed, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's hear him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Mr. Dordic, if you had opened the right-hand door on Tunnel 9 and you were looking into the tunnel, would this be an accurate depiction of how the detainees were forced to sit in the tunnel, all on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
