utterances.text: Yes, mostly. When someone was not hurt or when the guards were not there, we had to sit on the left-hand side, too, sometimes when the guards were not there, because it was so tight. There wasn't enough room.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Any time the guards were around or the door was open or closed, this would be an accurate depiction of how you were sitting but many times you had to have your head down; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Our heads between our knees and our arms on our knees, sufficiently as the drawing is, only our knees were more bent and our heads were leaning on our knees. It all depended on what the guard was ordering us to do.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. I'm finished with the drawing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I assume that the diagram will be admitted into evidence since she has shown it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I was just using it for identification purposes. I will tender it to the court if they like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Well, what were you identifying?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I was identifying the position of the detainees in Tunnel 9, how they sat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Generally, or this particular witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, he admitted that that is the way they sat when people came, except that they had their heads down. So I don't know that it's totally accurate, but if Ms McHenry would like to introduce it into evidence, I'll be happy to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: If you wish to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: We now offer this drawing into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be document D8/1 and D9/1.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. So basically you were somewhere at least halfway down the tunnel and there were about three feet or 1 metre worth of stairs on the outside of the door looking out; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Three or four steps. I don't know exactly how many there were, because believe me, I had many other problems to be able to think about the number of steps, and I was sitting -- let me repeat again -- roughly in the middle of the tunnel. I can't say that I sat exactly in the middle. I didn't measure it, but I think that's where I was.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Was Mirko Kuljanin also in Tunnel 9 with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mirko Kuljanin?

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Excuse me. We need to wait until the court finishes talking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: It's a private aside.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry. Was Mirko Kuljanin also in Tunnel 9 with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember. I can't recall which Mirko you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: He's an older gentleman from Bradina. His name is Mirko Kuljanin. You don't remember him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this moment I can't recall exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now going to Slavko Susic, today your first statement was that the person who took him out was Esad Macic, and I'm not finished forming the question yet, but in your statement of 1994 in Belgrade and in your statements to the Prosecution of 1996 you never mentioned Mr. Landzo's name in connection with Slavko Susic, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise if I said that again today. I said that Esad Macic was frequently a guard outside Tunnel Number 9, but as far as my memory is correct, I said that I remember it was Hazim Delic and Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: But you never said that in any of your prior statements, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Statements take a long time and maybe even now I will not be able to say everything I should have said and all I have gone through.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, your Honours, I'm going to ask some questions now about a witness that they had sought protection for but I believe that there's no issue on that now, but just to be sure, I want to know -- Ms McHenry knows I am going into the issue of some brothers. Do they still have protection or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I believe it has been verified that they do not -- that there is no protection at least with respect to -- only one of them is a potential witness. He is not protected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In fact, he appeared on the television.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That's exactly right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: That's the one. So I'm going to go forward with questions about him. Thank you. Was there an order in force with his protection because I don't want to violate any order if there was and I want to make it clear whether there is an order still in effect or no order in effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I believe the order, if I'm correct, indicates that the Prosecution or if the witness withdraws his request for protection, and this witness, Mr. Vaso Dordic, has withdrawn his request for protection.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, Mr. Dordic, the Dordic brothers, the twins, are cousins of yours, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. Which twin brothers are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Vaso and Veseljko Dordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know there's two years difference between them. They're not twins at all.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. So they're just brothers; they're not twins?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, brothers.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: When they were in Hangar Number 6, you were in Tunnel Number 9; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: And both of these boys are mentally retarded, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't say that, but they didn't complete elementary school. They were not very good students. They are introverted. They didn't go to any special school for mentally retarded people. They went to regular school, which they did not finish. They finished it later on as evening classes. They did their military service, regular Yugoslav national service.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dordic, I didn't ask you those questions just then, but you and Ms McHenry had discussed this potential subject coming up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Your question was that they were mentally retarded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: And your answer was they have done their military service.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: But he also said he has never stated they were mentally retarded before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: He has not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I have his statement from 1994 shown to him in Serbian, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I don't have a copy of the Serbian version, but in the English version I would like for impeachment purposes to show him he stated under oath, where the statement had been read back to him and he had an opportunity to correct it, that the brothers are retarded. I would like to have that document provided to him in Serbian right now -- I mean in Bosnian, if I could. Madam Residovic, do you have a copy of it? If you don't mind --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I don't know what that means. Even now all he is saying they have gone through all these classes and then have had their military training. Retarded persons cannot do all that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, your Honour, I believe his statement on the record was that he had never said they were retarded before. This is impeachment purposes. He did state that in his sworn testimony before the judge in Belgrade. So I would like to have the opportunity to ask the usher to please show him his statement from Belgrade in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't object to him being shown something. I will just clarify. As far as I know it wasn't under oath and when he said he had never stated that he was referring to today, but I certainly don't have any objection to him being shown something for impeachment purposes to clarify the matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What page, please, so that I don't waste your time?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes. It's a different page in the English version, so I'm trying to find out what page it is in your version. Would you please refer to page 13 of your statement there, please? Page 13, fifth paragraph down. I'm going to go read it in English and when they translate to you in Bosnian, you tell me if this has been interpreted correctly, please. The fifth paragraph: "When I arrived in Number 6 I saw my two relatives, Veseljko and Vaso Dordic, who are retarded".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Gentlemen, maybe that is how it was noted in Belgrade. I repeat again that when I made the statement in Belgrade it was only fifteen days or so that I had left the camp, so I can't claim anything like that, because they didn't go to any special school. I can't claim that they were retarded. If they didn't complete elementary school, and I think that something is not quite all right with them, because, after all, elementary education was obligatory and they didn't manage to complete it, though later on they did through courses, evening classes, and they did their military service normally, and they also worked normally. My personal opinion is that they were at a lower intellectual level.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Did you say they were at a lower intellectual level. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: As compared to him. As compared to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask him to look at the first page, too, that this was a document that was given by him before a judge in the lower court in Belgrade on October 17th, 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: At the time that you gave in a statement it was given in Serbian and written in Serbian -- I mean Bosnian, Serbo-Croatian, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose this is his opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You were read the statement back and you had an opportunity to correct it, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but maybe I didn't remember to correct that. I'm not a doctor. How can I claim that anyone is mentally retarded? It was just my opinion that they were at a somewhat lower level than normal people.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me go on to after you were released from Celebici and taken to Musala, Mr. Landzo was a guard at Musala, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: And while you were you never saw him beat anyone, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. In Musala, no.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: In fact, as a prisoner at Musala you were given a lot of freedom. You were allowed to work outside the prison, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My actual position gave me freedom and if I did not have the ability to do these things that I did, I wouldn't be given any freedom, but I did move around because of the job I was assigned to do in front of the prison.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: And the job that you were assigned to do was that you repaired and worked on army and police automobiles, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: And you saw Mr. Landzo every day while you were there at Musala, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every day while he was a guard there I saw him. I don't think he stayed there as a guard for long, but I saw him later also, when he was a prisoner in Musala.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: While he was a guard there, he gave you some cigarettes and an alcoholic drink and you all became friendly, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm not hearing any interpretation at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On one occasion --

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: I didn't hear any of that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly repeat your answer so that it should be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were not friends at all while he was a guard, because the director of the prison --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHITE
utterances.text: I am still not hearing the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Brocica --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Let's hear.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear now? Can you hear now, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. Kindly let's hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I was saying that we were not friends while he was a guard, because the manager explicitly prohibited any mistreatment for me, because I'd move around, but later when Landzo was imprisoned in the sports hall, one floor below us, because at the time we were on the second floor and they were on the ground floor, Landzo behaved differently as compared to the time when he was a guard in the camp. It is true that he would give me cigarettes. I can't remember the alcohol, but on one occasion he said that he admired all Serbs who managed to survive camp Number 6 and Number 9 in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Mr. Dordic, you stated in your statement also that you were in very poor condition when you were released and that you gave the statement in 1994 that your memory was not so good. Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Then in your statement to the Prosecution you stated also that so much time has passed that your memory wasn't so accurate then either. Didn't you state that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Considering that it is now, what, five years since the events in the Celebici camp and there are so many data to be given. So I apologise if something is not absolutely correct. I'm not a computer to remember absolutely every date and every name.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dordic. I pass the witness, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we can have a break for 30 minutes now and we will come back at 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Let's have the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: May it please your Honour, Mr. Dordic, I want to ask you a few questions and I hope to be reasonably quick, so we will finish as soon as possible with you; all right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. Dordic, you have talked a little earlier on today about the length of time that you were in detention all told. Would it be right that, in fact, it came to a total of about two and one-third years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll tell you exactly the period. I don't know the amount of time but between 30th May 1992 and 4th October 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And I've calculated that, and you can correct me if you want to, but I think that's about two and one-third of a year. Would that be about right? Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Somewhere around there. I did not calculate exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I don't want to take you back into the exact number of days, Mr. Dordic, but I just want to establish the rough period. Mr. Dordic, very shortly after your release you went and gave a statement to the court at Belgrade before Judge Semic, I think it was. Do you remember doing that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Help me about that: that was on 17th October 1994. Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would you also accept this: when you went to the court in Belgrade and made that statement you were at the time suffering from both physical illness and mental illness? Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say that it was an illness, a mental illness, but I have to say that in that period and the following eight months after I was released from prison, I was sleepless. Every night when I would go to sleep images from the camp would come back, and for eight months I basically did not sleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I don't want to ask you about the physical manifestations of ill health, Mr. Dordic, but can I just pin you down to this: your health had been -- your mental health had been seriously damaged at that time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By virtue of my not having enough sleep I was very tired, and I had nightmares, which are recurring to date, not as often, not as frequently as at that time, but it happens when I'm reminded of these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'll do my best not to remind you too much of them, Mr. Dordic, but I'm going to have to ask you one or two questions, and I'm sure you don't mind that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's very kind of you. Would you help me, please, about this: was one of the features of your being unwell during that period finding that your memory was playing tricks with you and your memory was not quite as accurate as it used to be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is for sure. My memory and my mental capacity have been eroded by the events there. That is the first trauma and the first tragedy and this is also the first Tribunal before which I am appearing in my life, so all that together.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I want to make it plain to you that I'm not criticising you in any way. You understand that, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So the problems that you had with memory and so on, were they at their worst in the eight months after your release?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. For the most part these problems took place in that period. After that I started getting more sleep and I started working and getting back to normal life, and I think that today I am a regular person when I'm not reminded of these events, when I'm out of touch -- when I'm not in touch with these issues, but every reminder of my stay here, the people who were there as prisoners and as witnesses, you know, leaves ugly memories.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So the problem hasn't entirely cleared up even now; is that what you are saying to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, if I had another 70 lives, regular human lives, I don't think that I would be able to forget this, not all of it. I'm forgetting details, but the essence of everything that I went through that, I experienced, is there to stay. It may just be pushed back into the subconscious. It may not show up in regular life but the essence is essence. I was humiliated there in every respect, as a human being, as a person and physically and health wise, and I can't forget that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I understand all that, Mr. Dordic, but can you just help me about this: what you are saying is that you remember the broad facts of what happened, but as regards details of, for example, places and dates and people, that's something where you can't be entirely accurate; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As you yourself said, I was there for 28 months or however long it was, and I cannot remember all details at one time. There are -- there may not be a human being on this planet who could be able to do that and under the conditions that I was in. I remember the things that I remember and I hope that you will not take badly things that I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Let me make it plain to you, Mr. Dordic, I'm not criticising you in any way at all, but can I give you an example of how serious mistakes can be made about dates and so on? You initially told the Belgrade judge that you had been released in October 1994 and then in a subsequent statement you said you had been released in December 1994. Do you remember making that mistake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I have paper of the International Red Cross of the date when I was exchanged. I think I actually have it with me in The Hague. It states the date when I was exchanged, that is released from the prison. The only thing that comes to mind is that there must have been a mistake, and the exact date is 4th -- it started on 4th and it was completed by 6th, but in the release document of the International Red Cross it states 4th October 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. The place where you've told us that it was December 1994 was the statement that you made to the Office of the Prosecutor in January 1996 and you then subsequently corrected it in a further statement. Do you remember doing that, going back and correcting it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I probably do remember. It must have been in Belgrade, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Well, will you accept from me that that's the sequence of events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you. That's very kind, Mr. Dordic. Again, I don't want to ask about physical difficulties that you had but did you receive treatment from a doctor in relation to your mental difficulties, the problems you were having with nightmares and so on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean when I came from the camp?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes, after being released from the camp did you receive some treatment for having nightmares and things like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I only took sun (sic), which are some tablets, some tranquillisers, because at that time I had some other problems. I did not have a place to live. I did not have a job. So I was not thinking whether I was sleeping or not sleeping. I was more concerned about what I was going to eat the next day, because we had left everything -- we had lost everything in that war. So I did not have time for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Who did you get the drugs from? A doctor or a chemist's or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly from a pharmacist.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: But some you got from a doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Who was the doctor? Can you tell us that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first once I received from Dr. -- this was still in Konjic. Let me remember the name of him. That was in the prison still. My memory is failing me right now. A doctor who was a Muslim, and also from the Catholic church in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm really interested in the period after your release and going back to Serbia, Mr. Dordic. Can you remember who the doctor was there who prescribed any drugs for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was Dr. Bjelica in Belgrade, in Bajanica Kosa, and doctors in the city where I resided at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: How long did you continue taking the drugs for, Mr. Dordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not take them regularly, only when I felt the need to take them, but basically over the period of eight months, but not all the time. Just when I needed to, I would take a pill.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Have you had to take drugs since the period of eight months has elapsed? Do you take drugs at all now for the problems you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can you help me about this: you mentioned Dr. Bjelica. Have you had any contact with the Serbian refugee organisation since your release from Celebici and Musala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What organisation do you have in mind specifically?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Have you had any contact with any organisations that purport to represent the interests of Serbian refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I first arrived in Belgrade, I went to my uncle, who lived near New Belgrade. My sister took me to Dr. Bjelica, myself and two cousins and a brother-in-law. We all went to Dr. Bjelica, because Dr. Bjelica is from our region. He was born in the Konjic area. So we went and had a check-up there. He said that he -- nothing -- he couldn't help us with anything more than these tablets for sleep, because it was too late to treat all the other consequences. So he just gave us these sleeping pills. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Have you continued to have contact with Dr. Bjelica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I met him several times in the Association of Detainees in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: It is about the Association that I wanted to ask you. When did you last meet Dr. Bjelica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Last time it was about a month ago, when he was to come here to testify before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And help us about this: where did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, as I say, in the premises of this Association. That is the place where we sort of come -- we come by this place for information regarding our -- regarding possibilities of our residence within the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and some humanitarian issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can you just tell us, this was the office of the organisation in Belgrade proper or New Belgrade, or where exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is in Belgrade proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is that the main offices of the organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is no other office. It's just one office. It's not even our own. We just have it -- we're given it to use for our meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is it inside another building that's got another organisation in it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know what else is in there, what's upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is it a government building, Mr. Dordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Serbia most things are State or government-run. I don't know this particular one. We are an association of detainees and we are part of it, as well as people who sympathise with our cause and who are trying to assist and help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. Can you just tell us this, please: what is the street name and street number in which the Association meets?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't -- if the witness knows, I have no objection to his answering, but just I would ask that it be in private session, just to make sure that later on if there's some incident at the association, it is not because its address was publicised. So I have no objection, if the witness knows, his stating that, but I would just ask that it be done in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I am entirely in your Honour's hands. I suspect it is probably information that is fairly easy to come by but if my learned friend insists on it, it is a matter for her and your Honours as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHITE
utterances.text: I never thought it was any secret association, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: It is definitely not a secret association, I have no idea. They may well not object to us giving it publicly. Just in case there would be some later on harassment or something and then the Tribunal would be criticised. Without then checking I don't know if it's public or not. Just to be extra cautious, I think it's advisable to have the actual address in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I am told by one of the computer buffs along the line here they publish all their details on the Internet. So I rather think it is a case of closing the stable door after the horse has bolted many, many months ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If that's correct ... I have no information.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I am desperate not to give information, certainly not hearsay information from down the line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Except you have anything in particular against the Association, I don't see the relevance of all these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I am going to find out exactly what the nature of his meetings with the good doctor are. Your Honour will recall that we raised this matter a week ago. I am entitled to investigate matters that relate to the potential credibility or otherwise of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You might have your way but I don't see the real merit in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If I'm wasting my time, then I'm terribly sorry, but I would respectfully submit that it's entirely relevant. Mr. Dordic, what sort of things do you discuss when you go to these meetings at the refugee organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The thing is that the detainees would get together to meet and the idea was to have a place where we could all get together, because we are now scattered around the globe, and also there are a number of people who want to help us, and there is no other way. There is no other form to assist us if not through an organisation, and if they want to get in touch with somebody, and even this Tribunal got in touch with the Association, and thanks to this Association and to this phone line, otherwise it would be very difficult to find even me in Serbia had it not been for this Association.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Could you just help us about the street address? I got distracted for a moment. Can you tell us what the street address is, please, in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If the Trial Chamber deems that this is necessary, I am prepared to say it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I would like you to answer, please, unless I'm stopped from so doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You can tell him the number, for what it is worth.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can I just add that if the witness has information indicating that the address is confidential, he can then ask for it to be in private session. I have no information one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the street number where the Association office is?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Dordic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The number is 101.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And the street name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Keneza Milosza, Prince Milosz.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I would like you to look at three pictures please and tell us if you know the people in them. These are photographs that I have shown to my learned friend Ms McHenry. if I can make this plain what these are, these are scanned images from the video that your Honours saw last week. Mr. Dordic, I would just like you to look at each of the photographs in turn, please. (Handed) do you recognise that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It's written there very well. It's Dr. Bjelica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: We like to try to make the questions easy, Mr. Dordic. All right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Look at the second photograph, please. Do you recognise that lady?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is even clearer here. The letters are even clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: What is the name of that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr.s Dusitsa Bojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Have you ever met her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Several times I have been with her.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Look at the third photograph, please: I think his name is Starsivic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mirdrak Starsivic. Again the name is written down. I met him only once.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only once. Recently in Belgrade, I think. As for Mr.s Bojic, we have become very good friends and she has helped me a great deal in finding my way round in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: During the course of these various meetings that you have had with representatives of that organisation, Mr. Dordic, have you discussed the evidence that other people have already given in this case at any time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we don't have that much time. When I go to the Association I spend half an hour, have a cup of coffee, enquire about things I personally am interested in, like my status in Yugoslavia, and other things of a humanitarian nature. I don't spend that much time there to be able to discuss our testimonies.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Have you ever seen anybody else discussing their future evidence with the people at the organisation, Mr. Dordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Have you ever been to Romania, Mr. Dordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: When did you go to Romania?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we were giving that statement for Mr. Bart.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Whereabouts in Romania did you go to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the town of Timosoira.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: How many people went there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly but all people who had evidence to give. I think about fifteen of us. I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: When you saw Dr. Bjelica about a month ago, did you talk about the case with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Not at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Basically no. He said that he was going too. I didn't have time. As I said, I have started to work and to lead a normal life in Yugoslavia, so that I don't have time for ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Let's move on to another topic, please. I want to ask you about Mr. Mucic and some of your dealings with him. You saw him approximately 20 times in all at the camp; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Normally at the entrance to whichever building it was you were being kept in at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, or at the entrance, or if I was going out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And was that invariably day-time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And your evidence last week was this, but can we just recap on it, please: you said when he was in the camp there was discipline; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Much greater discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And when he was in the camp, no-one came in to beat you or to mistreat you. That's right, isn't?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think after all that Mr. Mucic was present at one beating-up in this canal in front of building Number 9. He wasn't very close. He wasn't on the spot, but he was a bit further removed, and a guard -- I think his name was Buric, he filmed the beatings that we were getting with a camera.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Dordic, you said to their Honours that you think that that's the case, but you're not sure, are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm saying that it is difficult to be sure of something while you're being beaten. I can't claim 100 per cent that he was there, but it seemed to me that it was him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The reason you told us last week that: "When he was in the camp, no-one came in to beat us", the reason was this: there were groups of people who would go into the camp, such as MUP and the HVO and a group called Agrepi; is that right? They were the people that would beat people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably in Building Number 6. In Number 9 at the very beginning some very strong people would come in, saying that they came from Grude. They beat Velimir and Desimir Mrkajic outside, but Mucic was not with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I want to ask you now about the incident at the manhole that you have told us about. It is right, isn't it, that you were unconscious through a lot of that incident. Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is logical, as I had no air down there. When I came out, I came to and I felt them beating me again, and I saw Mucic. He was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Well, you have told us in evidence last week that you were not fully aware of what was going on because of the lack of oxygen, Mr. Dordic, and that's the case, isn't it? You didn't know fully what was going on around you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I said when I came out I got oxygen. This was a little later, maybe ten minutes later.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You became hysterical, then a panic attack; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You see, I suggest to you that you have entirely mistaken the presence of Mr. Mucic at any such incident, Mr. Dordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know, but I think there must be other witnesses who can testify to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would you accept that you may be wrong about Mr. Mucic's presence in that incident, Mr. Dordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that I am not wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: But you may be?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: How many times will you ask that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I object. He stated that he saw Mr. Mucic there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: He has confirmed it. You don't have to follow that up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe I wasn't even alive over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Dordic, the incident where you say you went to work at Mr. Mucic's house, do you accept that in none of the three statements that you made did you relate that incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember whether I mentioned it in my statements, but I remember well. If you want me to, I can explain the details. I remember well the well equipped garage belonging to Mucic, which I saw open when I was there and Mr. Mucic, who was just woken up, and he came out. I think my brother was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. Dordic, the question I asked you was: do you accept that you had not mentioned it in any of the statements that you had made?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Asked and answered. The witness says he doesn't remember if he mentioned it in the prior statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Was the first time that you had ever mentioned it today in effect, wasn't it, or have you discussed it with Mr.s McHenry before?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Objection. The witness has just stated he doesn't remember if he even mentioned it in his statement, so I think to ask him when exactly the first time he mentioned it is not fair. He has already said he doesn't remember exactly if and when he first mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: All right. I have no further questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Any other cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): I apologise, your Honours: I'll put my papers on the rostrum as soon as I put on my headphones. Your Honours, if I may continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. The witness is available to you. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you. Good afternoon, Mr. Dordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Edina Residovic. I am defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pleased to meet you.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I know you must be tired from our questions by now. My colleagues have asked you many of the questions that I wanted to ask you, so that they have facilitated the task for both you and me, and therefore I would like to ask you to answer the questions I put to you, if you can, as concisely and as clearly as possible. In answer to a question from the Prosecution you gave some personal information about yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please tell me whether it is correct that you are the son of Simo and Radoika and your mother's surname was Ivazic, that you were born on December 31st, 1968 in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That you are an electronics technician?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And that until the war you worked in the railway enterprise Sarajevo, the work unit at Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So these are your complete personal data?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In answer to questions put to you by my colleagues you said that you were very familiar with Bradina, so that you know every stone, as you yourself said today; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You had members of the family, relatives in Bradina and friends?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you knew many people personally in Bradina; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: More or less everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, when on April 24th you came to Bradina, you came among friends and you had where to stay, you had a place to stay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have also testified that when you came to Bradina on April 24th, the barricades had already been put up on the surrounding hills and in Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Guard, watch duty. Watch duty, yes, not barricades. The difference is considerable and I must say that everyone could pass through those barricades, as you call them, on condition that they were unarmed, but arms could not pass through those points. These points were just for control purposes. There were two points on the highway.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is exactly what I wanted to ask you. Therefore, at both checkpoints or rather barricades on the main road, which you had under your control, representatives of the Territorial Defence, the police or armed citizens could not pass by; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In answer to a question from the Prosecution you said that while keeping watch duty you were armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you clarified that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For the same reasons all others who were on watch duty were also armed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For reasons of personal security, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You answered also that a kind of defence had been organised in Bradina and that heading it was Rajko Dordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was the self-organisation of the people as a struggle for their survival.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The people elected a crisis staff of Bradina; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In answer to one of the questions you mentioned the names of Vaso Vujicic, Dragan Vujicic and Vukasin Mrkajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Those are people that you know personally; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You know personally that Vukasin Mrkajic was President of the SDS of Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that he was.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Though, as you said, you did not attend meetings, you knew that these persons that you mentioned from personal contacts with them were part of the leadership of the Defence of Bradina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I should like to ask with the help of the Registry if you could show this name to the Prosecution and then to the witness in view of the fact that it is a protected witness, so I do not wish to mention him by name. (Handed to Prosecution and witness) Until this name is shown to you may I ask: is it correct that Bradina is on the main highway between Konjic and Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And that stopping the traffic prevents the normal flow of traffic from Sarajevo to Konjic and vice versa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This witness K, according to your personal knowledge, was a member of the crisis staff in Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably. I'm not 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You confirmed that watch duty was kept all around Bradina in an area of about 20 kms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the circle around Bradina. If one were to draw it out into a straight line I think it would be about 20 kms.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And all the people who were keeping watch duty were armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the Prosecution in January 1996 in Timosoira you stated that Bradina was attacked for the first time on May 13th and that as far as you know, the Commander of that attack was Stranko Zovko; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: May I say he is a commander of HVO based in Podrazic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what I learned about him but let me tell you what prompted the people most to organise the Defence of Bradina. After the meeting of the crisis staff in Podrazic held with Mr. Zovko and I don't know who else, Zovko stated allowed -- at least that's what I heard -- that he would burn down Bradina, that not a stone would be left unturned in Bradina.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Probably after that you started digging the trenches that you referred to this morning and to prepare yourself more seriously for the Defence of Bradina; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally was a witness not of military activities but civilian activities in Zukici next to my house. I personally witnessed an ordinary transport truck of -- a FAP truck that was transporting weapons below my house and driving the weapons away to a point from where Bradina could be attacked. So I personally observed this, and all this prompted me to seek shelter, because it was not normal to see so many weapons in the hands of another ethnic group, and nobody warned me or offered or invited me to join any kind of army or defence against I don't know whom and I don't know what from among the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kuljanin (sic), when you reached Bradina on 24th, for some time you continued working at the railways; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I apologise. You made a lapse. My name is not Kuljanin. I'm Dordic.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I'm sorry, Mr. Dordic. For some time you continued working at the railways?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you were living and staying at your friend's house, Janko Glogovaz?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Janko Glogovaz is probably known to everyone. He was a teacher in the elementary school in Bradina.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the rail transportation ceased on 21st April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whether the date is correct I can't say but somewhere around then, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know why the traffic came to a halt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because war operations start in Sarajevo of major proportions.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dordic, you also confirmed that you learned from the radio of significant military operations in Sarajevo and Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. One could hear it very well in Bradina and Ivan Sedlo, because we couldn't -- we didn't have electricity for a long time. We were switched off, so we couldn't listen to the radio.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also stated that in the area where you were keeping watch duty you had dug ten trenches. In an earlier statement it was 12 but that isn't important. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't dig ten. I dug out one for myself.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you did dig out one but you said in that area there were about ten trenches. Other local people keeping watch duty in other areas in this total area of some 20 kms were also digging similar trenches; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whoever had any common sense and who wanted to protect oneself from the attacks of the other side probably did. I wasn't there, but I only know what happened where I was.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were digging this trench for yourself, for an upright position, in the village of Veloviz near Zukici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not a village; it's a locality.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it is in the direction of Zukici going from Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me where did you normally keep watch duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said there.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So during the battles from 25th-26th May you were there, too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You heard that the defence line had been broken through, so with Mladen Dordic and Dusko Koprivitsa, you headed for the centre of Bradina at first; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We were left alone and we fled towards Bradina. We saw there was no-one else and so we fled towards the centre of Bradina. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you disarmed there two TO members from your village, but after some shooting you threw away their weapons and they went off?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that is not correct. They were two of my friends, two neighbours from Zukici, Javo Adam and Alvadin Resvanovic. I'm not concealing their names. We were drinking water at a stream and they came up to us. It is true we have took their weapons away. We were afraid that they might use them against us. We sat down. If you don't believe me, ask them. We lit some cigarettes taken from them. They were called York, of Croatian manufacture. Somebody had brought them in. We didn't have any cigarettes in Bradina for some time. We sat down and we talked. Me and Adam Javo were very good friends. I asked: "Why did all of this have to happen?" He was in a panic just like me. He didn't believe everything that was happening or at least that was the impression I had, that he was confused. So we had a cigarette each. We picked up our weapons. They went in the direction of Zukici and we headed for Bradina. We threw away the weapons, that is true, and some of them or some other military people threw a bomb or a shell fell very near us. Anyway I don't know. In any event we ran.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Also, Mr. Dordic, you stated this morning that as far as you were able to notice, the strength of the attack during the battle was directed towards one part of the positions and that there was a lot of noise to intimidate your forces; is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but the noise was concentrated in the centre of the village of Bradina and the inhabited areas, so that there were few houses that were spared shelling, so that it was exclusively inhabited places that were shelled, that were targeted, places where civilians live normally.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dordic, though you were a commander of a detachment you said that during that battle you did not take part in the fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't understand very well.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were a commander of a squad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is not true.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Will you show me the document where this is stated?

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have just told us that orders were given by word of mouth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I was not a commander. There were no commanders.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that Dragan Vujicic was a detachment-platoon commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the person who transferred information in that area around the railway station.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And Nedjo Dragultenovic was the Commander of a company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Of a detachment. Though there were 350 of you, as you said this morning, you managed to resist this attack for 48 hours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We didn't hold back. It was not us. First of all, there was the artillery fire, which beat and hit the hills and increasingly the inhabited places, and it was out of fear, I think, that the attack went on for 48 hours. I think, though I am not a military expert, but to have so many people and being armed as they were, they could have defeated us and entered the town in a couple of hours. I think they feared entering Bradina.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dordic, you also said that you did your military service in the JNA and that you were in a communications unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You probably know much more about military information than I might know, because women in our country did not do any military service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, except exceptionally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: How long do you think we should continue? I didn't expect you to go as far as that. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, if we stay until 6 o'clock I will finish my cross-examination and I think perhaps it would be a good idea to finish with this witness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think so. That's why I want to assess how long you will take. You would like to finish with him today. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you. Therefore, as far as you know, and you certainly do know that operational and tactical groups in the JNA were exclusively linked to combat operations on the front; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I do not know much about military tactics. I learned more from my experience in the camp and later on when I was in Musala, more from that experience than from my military service. I had infantry training for only 20 days in the army.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you certainly knew from what you learned then and later that operational groups do not have anything to do with camps?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object. This witness has already stated he is not a military expert, so I object to further questioning about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Mr. Dordic, since you were a detainee in Celebici, you stated -- there was a problem with my interpretation. I all of a sudden got it in English. Now I can't hear anything. Let's try again. I think that I lost my interpretation. Mr. Dordic, this morning you stated that as a detainee you did not have any opportunity to know what people in Konjic ate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I knew very well the guards ate quite well.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But my question was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I can only say this --

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you, Mr. Dordic, did not have any information about what people in Konjic did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the most part, no. Only as related by the guards. That's how I found something out.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Personally you did not have information about who was where and who was in what duty in Konjic. You didn't know any of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dordic, you said that you learned some things from Zaro Mrkajic. Can you tell us whether Zaro Mrkajic was also a detainee in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Zaro Mrkajic, just like you, was not free to move around Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please if you could just answer my questions, maybe Zaro Mrkajic had an opportunity to contact other persons within the camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, with all persons in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Zaro Mrkajic also could get information from some third persons; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that what you heard from Zaro Mrkajic is something that he heard from third persons; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, what Zaro Mrkajic told you are neither your personal knowledge nor the personal knowledge of Zaro Mrkajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I --

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, thank you. That's enough, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could I just ask that the witness be permitted to finish his answer. It's not exactly clear to me because of the high speed, but to the extent that he has been cut off, for instance, with respect to the last question, I would ask that he be allowed to complete his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: What was the last question? Can you repeat it? MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Yes, I can. Mr. Dordic, your knowledge is not personally knowledge. You acquired them by hearing them from detainees, from Zaro Mrkajic, who also did not have personal knowledge but most probably heard of these things from third persons. Can you please answer this question with a "yes" or a "no"? Please just say "yes" or "no".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How can I answer "yes" or "no"? If you will allow me just to explain, your Honours, to clarify this yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking to you answer me with "yes" or "no". First of all, you said that Zaro Mrkajic did not have any personal knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am going to strenuously object. The witness has stated that he cannot fairly answer the question with a "yes" or "no". I strenuously object to the witness then being forced to do so. He must be allowed to give your Honours a full answer. This witness has answered large numbers of questions with a "yes" or "no" answer. This question he stated he cannot fairly do so, and I think it's improper for defence counsel to direct him to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think it is proper for counsel to observe the answers of witnesses is meant for the Trial Chamber. It's not for the personal consumption of counsel which are defence or Prosecution. All the answers are directed towards the administration of justice in this case. So where it is necessary to elaborate on an answer, I suppose it is better to leave him to do so. I agree in most cases you might prefer a "yes" or "no" answer, but there are cases where perhaps the witness might not be able to do that. So you don't have to press him too hard. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, I apologise if the witness or you had an impression that this was forced. As defence counsel of Zejnil Delalic I am interested in finding out the truth. It is in that regard that I'm asking my questions. So if you will allow me, I will re-state the question one more time. Maybe it will facilitate his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think so. To get an answer, you can still do so. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Mr. Dordic, Zaro Mrkajic is a detainee who had contacts with some -- with certain persons within the camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: He did not have freedom of movement outside of the Celebici camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: He did not have personal knowledge about persons and their duties in Konjic itself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, your Honours, may I have the permission to clarify this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Zaro Mrkajic is a detainee who could -- who was allowed to contact with everybody. I personally saw him talking to everybody, to Pavo Mucic, with Hazim Delic, with all the guards, and the knowledge, the information that he passed on to us was probably right, because -- and they are probably the words that he got from these people. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): In other words, Mr. Dordic, you assumed that Mr. Zaro Mrkajic found out the things that he told you from persons with whom he had contact in the prison; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not certain persons but the very persons who were in the administration of the camp and the guards.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is your assumption; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dordic, tell me whether in our language the word "boss" also stands for somebody who is well off?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that the guard Macic mentioned to you with respect of the missing food that the boss Delalic arrived, that is you believed that he was referring to Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I remember, he said "boss Delalic".

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dordic, you said that Mr. Delalic had a disco club in Konjic before the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also know that he was a well-off person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If you'll allow me, I will move on to another area of questioning relating to your departure from Bradina. With a group which included, as you said this morning, Mladen Dordic, Mirko Stravko, Radovan and Damian Dordic you left Bradina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think we were even more.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: May I assist you there? Radko, Jelenko and Mladen Kuljanin were also there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much for that reminder.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Also Zaro Mrkajic was among them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And it is also correct that until May 30th in difficult conditions with sleeplessness and without food you spent looking for a way to Kalinovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A road to salvation and it wasn't so much Kalinovic. When we looked back we saw Bradina in flames, so we had no place to turn back to.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dordic, before your surrender or turning over of weapons or capture, however you would like to define it, following May 30th, the afternoon -- until the afternoon of 31st May, when you arrived in Celebici, according to your own testimony you spent over 24 hours travelling there, and all this time you were subject to torture and mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and if your Honours will allow me to clarify this and prove the truthfulness of what I have to say --

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In Ljuta, Sabici, throughout this journey in Zepe, Verdulija you were beaten with different objects and also kicked with boots and with anything that was at hand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in your previous statement you stated that most people were already unconscious and beaten up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say that we were beaten unconscious when we were pretty much all standing up on our feet and receiving more beatings. You cannot call this an unconscious state. It is -- you can call it that we were in a state of besides ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Serbian language is fairly rich in these expressions. What I quoted here was because it had not been transmitted to me very precisely what you had actually said at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dordic, you stayed in Celebici until -- can you please help us and tell us when you -- how late you stayed in Celebici before you moved to Musala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was late October or early November. I think that the date was 17th. It was something 17th. I don't know if it was October or November. It just popped in my mind now.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you will agree with me that for your lack of ability to recall the date when questioned in Belgrade before the investigating magistrate as well as today, you gave different dates of your transfer from Celebici to Musala. In some instances you said it was October and in some you said it was November; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not claim with certainty that it was one or the other. I just said that it was around there. I was the next to last group that was moved from Celebici to Musala.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also clarified before the Trial Chamber, Mr. Dordic, why you have lapses in memory with respect to the statement you gave on 17th October 1994 in front of the judge in Belgrade. Could you tell me, Mr. Dordic, whether at that time you were questioned for about four hours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I apologise. I didn't hear when?

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before Judge Semic in Belgrade on 17th November 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was even longer than four hours. I think it could have been more like six hours.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If the statement says that it started at 1.20 and was -- and finished in 4.50, then maybe what was written down reflects shorter period of time than was the actual time of your questioning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did not take into account the breaks that we had taken.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were reminded that you were under obligation to seek the truth and that the consequences of speaking untruths was a criminal offence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And in this statement you have mentioned a number of persons and individuals from Konjic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is probably so.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also knew the duties that they were discharging at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In that statement you never mentioned Zejnil Delalic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember. I may have.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If you would like to refresh your memory, I could produce this statement for you to look at, but if I say so, will you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And also you never knew personally Zejnil Delalic before the war. You only knew of him as the owner of the disco club?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I knew his face, but never knew him in person. I had never met him in person.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Mr. Delalic for the first time in Timosoira because the investigator d'Hooge asked you about him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At that time you said that he was a Mafioso?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the story that was circling around before the war on the eve of the war, that he spent a lot of time in Austria and that he was engaged in all kinds of shady dealings.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After your release from the prison you, as you already stated, said that you were -- you had the opportunity to visit repeatedly the offices of the Association of Detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And a number of you gave statements in Timosoira?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You knew that the Prosecutor of the International Tribunal had issued an indictment which included Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The press in Serbia as well as the television there frequently covered the work of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't recall any of the broadcasts, but informations from here did make it to the television.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And from these sources later you found out about the duty, the post that Mr. Delalic had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The information I had, this was information I acquired in the Celebici camp and the Musala camp, as I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dordic, you were questioned for the first time in Celebici and you said that you were questioned by Stenek and Niksic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This statement was dictated to you and was taken down by Ismeta Postna, who was the stenographer and you described how you signed it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You answered truthfully the questions that were asked of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, I made an effort to speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And all this was typed up in your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say that I have listened or read this statement because, as you yourself said, we were -- I am conscious that's not what I said, but we were sort of beside ourselves. We were in constant fear of being beaten, because there was a huge fellow standing behind me throughout the taking of this statement.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you gave the statement the first day you arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After that you never gave a statement in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The next statement you gave in January 1993, when you were in Musala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise but I don't recall this statement.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When asked by my colleague McMurrey, you said that this was the fourth statement, if that is the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
